q: Which term describes the rule that protects a firm's assets from the personal creditors of its owners?
o: Limited liability, sometimes called defensive asset partitioning.
Entity shielding, sometimes called affirmative asset partitioning.
The charging order, which lets an owner's creditor take over the firm's management.
The exhaustion rule.
None of the above.
oe: Limited liability runs the other way. It shields the owners' personal assets from the firm's creditors.

Correct. Affirmative asset partitioning keeps firm assets for firm creditors, so an owner's personal creditor cannot seize the business's property. Even a general partnership, which has no limited liability, has this feature under RUPA's entity theory.
A charging order is a lien on the owner's distributions only. It gives the creditor no management rights and no claim to specific firm assets.
The exhaustion rule makes a firm creditor go after partnership assets before partners' personal assets. It protects partners, not the firm's assets.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Entity shielding

q: Under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001), what happens to a limited partner who takes part in managing the limited partnership's business?
o: The limited partner keeps the liability shield; the old control rule was largely eliminated (§ 303(a)).
The limited partner automatically becomes a general partner for all purposes.
The limited partner becomes liable for all partnership debts incurred after their first management decision.
The limited partner loses the shield only if they also contributed services rather than cash.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under earlier limited partnership acts, a limited partner who participated in control could be liable like a general partner. ULPA (2001) § 303(a) dropped that rule, so a limited partner is not liable for the partnership's obligations solely because they take part in management.
No act ever made participation convert a limited partner into a general partner for all purposes, and ULPA (2001) removed even the narrower control rule.
This overstates even the old control rule, which reached only creditors who reasonably believed the limited partner was a general partner.
The type of contribution has nothing to do with the limited partner's shield.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — ULPA (2001) control rule

q: Which of the following is required to create an agency relationship?
o: A contract supported by consideration.
An agreement that the agent will be paid.
A writing signed by the principal.
The principal's right to control.
None of the above.
oe: Agency needs consent, not a contract. Consideration is not required (Gorton v. Doty).
Gratuitous agents are common. Pay is not an element.
A writing is generally not required, except where the agent will sign contracts within the Statute of Frauds or the agency itself falls within it.

Correct. Agency requires the principal's manifestation, the agent's consent, and the principal's right to control. Control can be minimal, and the right to control, not its exercise, is what counts (R3d § 1.01).
D is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Elements of agency

q: Under the RUPA, which of the following does NOT by itself cause a partner's dissociation?
o: The partner's death.
The partner becoming a debtor in bankruptcy.
The partner's transfer of all of their transferable interest to a third party.
The partner's expulsion by a court for conduct that makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in partnership with them.
None of the above.
oe: Death is a dissociation event (§ 601).
Becoming a debtor in bankruptcy dissociates a partner (§ 601).
Correct. A transfer does not by itself cause dissociation (§ 503(a)(2)). It only gives the other partners the power to expel the transferor by unanimous vote (§ 601(4)(B)).
Judicial expulsion is a dissociation event (§ 601(5); Giles v. Giles Land Co.).
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Transfer is not dissociation

q: Under the Restatement (Third) of Agency, which of the following may an employee do while still employed, in preparation for leaving to compete with the employer?
o: Form a new limited liability company and sign a lease for office space.
Line up bank financing for the new business.
Ask the employer's customers to move their accounts to the new business once it opens.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Permitted. Preparing to compete is not a breach unless it is otherwise wrongful (R3d § 8.04).
Permitted. Arranging financing is preparation, not competition.
Not permitted. Soliciting the principal's customers during the agency is competing, not preparing (Bancroft-Whitney; Meehan).
Correct. Forming the entity, leasing space, and lining up financing are permitted preparation. Soliciting customers while still an agent breaches the duty of loyalty.
Soliciting customers during the agency is a breach, so C does not belong.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Preparing to compete

q: A buyout agreement pays a deceased partner's estate the partner's "capital account." Following G & S Investments v. Belman, how is that term generally read?
o: As the fair market value of the partner's share of the business.
As the value of the partner's share if the whole business were sold as a going concern.
As the book figure for the partner's capital account on the partnership's books.
As whatever amount a court finds fair at the time of death.
None of the above.
oe: Belman rejected a market-value reading. The term has a settled accounting meaning.
Going-concern value is the RUPA § 701 default for buyouts, not the meaning of "capital account" in an agreement.
Correct. Capital accounts are kept at book value, not market value. In Belman the figure was negative, so the estate received only $4,867.57, which shows the danger of book-value formulas.
Courts enforce buyout clauses as written. They do not substitute a fairness figure.
C is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Capital account formula

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: The Uniform Partnership Act (UPA) (1914) and the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997, as last amended in 2013 and printed in the supplement). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership with no written partnership agreement.

Which of the following is a feature of the aggregate theory that RUPA keeps?
o: A partnership may sue and be sued in its own name.
A partnership may own property in its own name.
Partners' personal liability for partnership debts.
The departure of any partner dissolves the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: This is an entity feature (RUPA § 307(a)).
This is an entity feature (RUPA § 203).
Correct. RUPA calls the partnership an entity (§ 201) but keeps partners' personal liability (§ 306(a)), along with pass-through tax treatment. These are the aggregate theory's leftovers.
That is the UPA's aggregate rule (§§ 29, 31). RUPA replaced it with dissociation, which need not dissolve the firm.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Aggregate leftovers in RUPA

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: The Uniform Partnership Act (UPA) (1914) and the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997, as last amended in 2013 and printed in the supplement). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership with no written partnership agreement.

Which statement correctly contrasts how partners hold specific partnership property?
o: Under the UPA a partner co-owns specific partnership property as a "tenant in partnership" (§ 25); under the RUPA a partner is not a co-owner of it (§ 501).
Under both acts, partners hold partnership property as tenants in common.
Under the RUPA a partner is a tenant in partnership; under the UPA the partnership alone owns the property.
Under both acts, a partner may sell an undivided share of a specific partnership asset to an outsider.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The UPA's aggregate view made partners co-owners with limited rights. The RUPA's entity view vests title in the partnership, so a partner has no interest in specific partnership property that can be transferred.
Neither act uses tenancy in common for partnership property.
This reverses the two acts.
Even under the UPA, tenancy in partnership was not assignable apart from the other partners' rights (§ 25(2)(b)), and under the RUPA there is nothing to sell.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Tenancy in partnership

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: The Uniform Partnership Act (UPA) (1914) and the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997, as last amended in 2013 and printed in the supplement). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership with no written partnership agreement.

Which statement correctly describes partners' personal liability for partnership obligations?
o: Under the UPA, partners are jointly and severally liable for all partnership obligations.
Under the UPA, partners are jointly liable for contract debts and jointly and severally liable for torts (§ 15); under the RUPA, they are jointly and severally liable for all obligations (§ 306(a)).
Under the RUPA, partners are only jointly liable for contract debts.
Under both acts, each partner is liable only for a pro rata share of each debt.
None of the above.
oe: The UPA split the rule: joint and several only for torts and breaches of trust.
Correct. The RUPA made liability joint and several across the board, but added the exhaustion rule: a creditor generally must pursue partnership assets first (§ 307(d)).
The RUPA abandoned the contract-only joint rule.
Neither act limits a general partner to a pro rata share as against outside creditors.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Joint vs. joint and several

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: The Uniform Partnership Act (UPA) (1914) and the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997, as last amended in 2013 and printed in the supplement). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership with no written partnership agreement.

Under which act does one partner's withdrawal from a three-partner firm, by itself, necessarily dissolve the partnership?
o: Under both the UPA and the RUPA.
Under the UPA only.
Under neither act.
Under the RUPA only.
Under either act, but only if the withdrawal is wrongful.
oe: Not under the RUPA. A withdrawal is a dissociation, and the § 603 switch sends it either to an Article 7 buyout or to Article 8 winding up.

Correct. Under the UPA's aggregate theory, any partner's departure dissolves the partnership (§§ 29, 31), though the business may continue in a new firm. Under the RUPA, dissociation does not necessarily cause dissolution.
Under the UPA, any partner's ceasing to be associated in carrying on the business dissolves the partnership (§ 29).
This reverses the acts.
Rightful or wrongful, a departure dissolves a UPA partnership; under the RUPA even a wrongful dissociation need not dissolve it.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Departure and dissolution

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: The Uniform Partnership Act (UPA) (1914) and the Revised Uniform Partnership Act (RUPA) (1997, as last amended in 2013 and printed in the supplement). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership with no written partnership agreement.

Which of the following statements about partners' fiduciary duties are true?
o: Under the UPA, a partner must account to the partnership for any benefit derived without the others' consent from any transaction connected with the partnership (§ 21).
The RUPA states the duties of loyalty and care in a list (§ 409) and adds a contractual obligation of good faith and fair dealing.
The RUPA lets a partnership agreement eliminate the duty of loyalty entirely.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. UPA § 21 was the main statutory loyalty rule; the rest came from common law such as Meinhard v. Salmon.
True. RUPA § 409(b) lists the loyalty duties, § 409(c) defines care, and § 409(d) adds good faith and fair dealing.
False. The agreement may narrow aspects of loyalty if not manifestly unreasonable, but may not eliminate it (§ 105(c)(5), (d)).
Correct. A and B are accurate statements of the UPA and RUPA approaches. C is wrong because § 105 forbids eliminating loyalty.
C is false.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Sources of partners' duties

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Actual authority under the Restatement (Third) of Agency (§§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 7, 26, 33–35).

Actual authority is judged from whose perspective?
o: The third party's reasonable belief, based on what the principal told it, about what the agent may do.
The principal's unexpressed intention.
The agent's reasonable understanding of the principal's manifestations to the agent.
Industry custom alone, regardless of anything the principal said.
None of the above.
oe: That is the test for apparent authority.
A principal's secret intent does not control. Mill Street's elders privately planned another helper, yet Bill still had implied authority.
Correct. Actual authority exists when the agent reasonably believes, based on the principal's words or conduct, that the principal wishes the agent to act (R3d §§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01).
Custom helps define implied authority, but an express instruction from the principal can override it as to actual authority.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Whose perspective

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Actual authority under the Restatement (Third) of Agency (§§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 7, 26, 33–35).

Which of the following can support a finding of implied actual authority?
o: The principal's past acquiescence in similar acts by the agent.
A trade custom that agents in this position take such steps.
An emergency in which the agent cannot reach the principal and must act to protect the principal's interests.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Prior practice is among the most important factors (Mill Street Church v. Hogan).
True. Custom can supply implied authority unless the principal says otherwise.
True. Emergencies are a recognized source of implied authority.
Incomplete. An emergency can also support implied authority.
Correct. Implied authority may come from prior conduct, custom, what is incidental or reasonably necessary to express duties, and emergencies.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Sources of implied authority

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Actual authority under the Restatement (Third) of Agency (§§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 7, 26, 33–35).

Which statement about termination of actual authority is true?
o: The principal may revoke it at any time, even in breach of its contract with the agent.
Ending actual authority automatically ends apparent authority as well.
Actual authority continues until the end of the agency contract's term, whatever the principal says.
An agent's breach of the duty of loyalty never affects the agent's authority.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The principal always has the power to revoke, though not always the right. A wrongful revocation still ends the authority but may leave the principal liable to the agent for breach of contract.
No. Apparent authority can linger until third parties have notice that the authority ended.
The principal's power to revoke is not limited by the contract term.
An agent's breach of fiduciary duty is one of the recognized ways actual authority can end.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Power vs. right to revoke

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Actual authority under the Restatement (Third) of Agency (§§ 2.01–2.02, 3.01) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 7, 26, 33–35).

An agent authorized to sell the principal's goods, with nothing more said, generally has implied authority to do which of the following?
o: Borrow money in the principal's name to fund the sale.
Give customary warranties and collect payment.
Settle unrelated lawsuits against the principal.
Sell the principal's other assets that were not placed with the agent.
None of the above.
oe: Borrowing is not incidental to selling goods.
Correct. Authority to sell carries implied authority to do what is incidental and customary, such as giving customary warranties and collecting payment.
Settling the principal's lawsuits has nothing to do with an authority to sell goods.
Authority to sell particular goods does not extend to other property.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Authority to sell

q: Under the RUPA, which of the following may be a partner in a general partnership?
o: A corporation.
An estate or a trust.
Another partnership.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. A partnership is an association of two or more "persons," and a corporation is a person.
True. Trusts and estates are persons under the RUPA's definition.
True. A partnership is itself a person that may be a partner in another partnership.
Incomplete. Trusts and estates may also be partners.
Correct. Individuals, corporations, LLCs, trusts, estates, and other partnerships are all persons who may associate as partners.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Who may be a partner

q: An employee injures a customer while following the employer's explicit instructions. Which statement is true under the Restatement (Third) of Agency?
o: Only the employer is liable, because the employee was following orders.
Only the employee is liable, because the employer did not commit the tort.
The employee is liable for their own tort, and the employer may be liable as well.
Neither is liable unless the customer first proves the employer was negligent in hiring the employee.
None of the above.
oe: Following orders is no defense. The agent is liable for its own torts (§ 7.01).
The employer may be directly liable for authorized conduct and vicariously liable for torts within the scope of employment.

Correct. An agent is subject to liability for its own tortious conduct even when acting with actual authority (§ 7.01). The principal can be directly liable for conduct it authorized (§ 7.04) and vicariously liable under respondeat superior (§ 7.07).
Respondeat superior is strict liability; no proof of the employer's own fault is needed.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Agent's own tort liability

q: How does the Restatement (Third) of Agency treat the Restatement (Second)'s concept of inherent agency power?
o: It keeps inherent agency power in the same form as R2d § 8A.
It abandons inherent authority and covers its cases mainly through apparent authority, estoppel, and a narrower rule for undisclosed principals (§ 2.06).
It extends inherent authority to all special agents.
It replaces inherent authority with strict liability for every act of every agent.
None of the above.
oe: The R3d drops the concept.

Correct. Section 2.06 makes an undisclosed principal liable when a third party detrimentally relies and the principal, on notice, failed to take reasonable steps to notify, and bars an undisclosed principal from relying on secret limits on authority. Watteau v. Fenwick-type cases now go through § 2.06.
Even the R2d tied the main inherent-authority rules to general agents and managers (§§ 161, 194–195).
Nothing in the R3d imposes such liability.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Inherent authority in the R3d

q: Under the RUPA, which statement about a filed statement of partnership authority (§ 303) is true?
o: A filed grant of authority is conclusive in favor of a person who gives value relying on it.
A filed limitation on a partner's authority is generally not notice to third parties, except a recorded limit on authority to transfer real property.
A filed limitation on authority binds every third party as soon as it is filed.
A and B.
B and C.
oe: True. A filed grant protects third parties who give value in reliance.
True. Filing a limit does not by itself bind outsiders in ordinary dealings; only a recorded limit on real-property transfers is deemed known (§ 103(d)(1)).
False. That would make every creditor search the records, which the RUPA does not require.
Correct. Grants of authority are conclusive for those who rely and give value; limits generally are not notice, except recorded limits on transferring real property.
C is false, and A is also true.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Statement of partnership authority

q: Under the Uniform Limited Liability Company Act (ULLCA) (2006, amended 2013), is a member of an LLC an agent of the company?
o: Yes, every member is an agent for any act in the ordinary course of the company's business, just as a partner is.
Yes, but only in a member-managed LLC.
No, not solely because they are a member of the LLC.
No, only the LLC's organizer may bind it.
None of the above.
oe: That is the RUPA rule for partners (§ 301), not the ULLCA rule for members.
The ULLCA does not make even members of a member-managed LLC agents by status.
Correct. ULLCA § 301(a) removes status-based agency. A member or manager may still have actual or apparent authority under ordinary agency principles.
The organizer's role ends with filing the certificate of organization; it has nothing to do with later authority.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Member is not an agent

q: Which statement about capacity in agency is correct?
o: The principal needs contractual capacity; the agent needs only minimal capacity.
Both principal and agent must have full contractual capacity.
Neither principal nor agent needs any capacity.
The agent must have contractual capacity, but the principal need not.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Because the agent's acts bind the principal, it is the principal who needs contractual capacity (R3d § 3.04). An agent needs only enough capacity to act (§ 3.05), so even a minor may serve as an agent.
An agent need not have contractual capacity.
A principal needs capacity; a minor's appointment of an agent is voidable.
This reverses the rule.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Capacity

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Choosing an entity. Compare the general partnership, the limited liability partnership (LLP), the limited partnership (LP), the limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), and the limited liability company (LLC), as each works by default.

Which of the following business forms may be created without any filing with the state?
o: A general partnership.
A limited liability partnership.
A limited partnership.
A limited liability company.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A general partnership needs no state action at all; it can even be formed without the parties intending to form one (RUPA § 202(a)).
An LLP requires a filed statement of qualification (RUPA § 901).
An LP exists only once a certificate of limited partnership is filed.
An LLC is formed by filing a certificate of organization (ULLCA § 201).
A is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Which entities need a filing

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Choosing an entity. Compare the general partnership, the limited liability partnership (LLP), the limited partnership (LP), the limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), and the limited liability company (LLC), as each works by default.

Which of these entities has two classes of owners by default?
o: The general partnership and the LLP.
The LLC.
The LLP and the LLC.
The LP and the LLLP.
None of the above.
oe: Both have only one class: general partners.
An LLC has one class of owners, members, though it may be member-managed or manager-managed.
Both have one class of owners.
Correct. Limited partnerships and limited liability limited partnerships have general partners, who manage, and limited partners, who invest.
D is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Classes of owners

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Choosing an entity. Compare the general partnership, the limited liability partnership (LLP), the limited partnership (LP), the limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), and the limited liability company (LLC), as each works by default.

Which statement about limited liability across these entities is correct?
o: General partners of an ordinary LP are shielded from the LP's debts.
In an LLLP and an LLC, every owner is shielded from the entity's debts by default.
Partners in an LLP remain personally liable for contract debts but not tort debts.
General partners in a general partnership are shielded once the firm keeps separate books.
None of the above.
oe: General partners of an LP have unlimited liability; that is why the LLLP form exists.
Correct. An LLLP shields its general partners as well as its limited partners, and an LLC shields all members and managers (ULLCA § 304). In an ordinary LP only the limited partners are shielded.
The RUPA LLP shield covers all partnership obligations incurred while it is an LLP (§ 306(c)), contract or tort.
Bookkeeping does not create limited liability. Only a filing (LLP, LP, LLLP, LLC) does.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Who has limited liability

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Choosing an entity. Compare the general partnership, the limited liability partnership (LLP), the limited partnership (LP), the limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), and the limited liability company (LLC), as each works by default.

By default, who manages each entity?
o: In an LP, all partners, general and limited, have equal management rights.
In an LLC, only managers appointed by the members may manage.
In a general partnership and an LLP, each partner has equal management rights; in an LP or LLLP, the general partners manage.
In a general partnership, partners vote in proportion to their capital contributions.
None of the above.
oe: Only general partners manage an LP.
An LLC is member-managed unless the operating agreement says otherwise (ULLCA § 407(a)).
Correct. Equal control is the default in general partnerships and LLPs (RUPA § 401(h)); in LPs and LLLPs, control belongs to the general partner; in LLCs it belongs to members or managers.
Equality applies regardless of how much capital each partner contributed.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Who controls

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Choosing an entity. Compare the general partnership, the limited liability partnership (LLP), the limited partnership (LP), the limited liability limited partnership (LLLP), and the limited liability company (LLC), as each works by default.

Which of the following are standard factors in choosing a business entity?
o: How each form is taxed.
Whether the owners can exit and cash out promptly.
Which fiduciary duties apply and whether they can be modified.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Pass-through versus entity-level tax is a central factor.
True. Exit and liquidity are listed selection factors.
True. The applicable duties, and how far the agreement may alter them, differ by entity.
Incomplete. Ability to exit and cash out is also a factor.

Correct. The listed factors include formation complexity, the right to manage, raising money, filing paperwork, avoiding personal liability, tax treatment, the ability to exit and cash out, and which fiduciary duties apply.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Selection factors

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Respondeat superior and the line between employees and independent contractors under the Restatement (Second) (§§ 2, 219–220) and the Restatement (Third) (§§ 7.03, 7.07).

Which of the following is NOT among the usual rationales for respondeat superior?
o: The employer controls, or has the right to control, the employee's work.
The employer can spread the cost of accidents through prices and insurance.
The employer's own fault in causing the injury.
The enterprise should bear risks characteristic of its activities.
None of the above.
oe: Control is a standard rationale.
Risk-spreading is a standard rationale.
Correct. Respondeat superior is strict liability without fault (Kerl). An employer's own negligence is a separate, direct-liability theory (R3d § 7.05).
Enterprise liability is the Bushey rationale.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Rationales for respondeat superior

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Respondeat superior and the line between employees and independent contractors under the Restatement (Second) (§§ 2, 219–220) and the Restatement (Third) (§§ 7.03, 7.07).

How did the Restatement (Third) change the Restatement (Second)'s master–servant terminology?
o: It renamed the servant an "employee" but kept the right-to-control test.
It replaced the right-to-control test with a test based on how the worker is paid.
It made every agent an employee.
It abolished respondeat superior for non-physical torts.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A master–servant relationship under the R2d became an employer–employee relationship under the R3d. The employer controls, or has the right to control, the manner and means of the work. The test is largely the same in new words.
Method of payment is one factor in the R2d § 220 list, not a replacement test.
Many agents are non-employee agents, such as an outside lawyer or a broker.
Respondeat superior still applies to employees' torts within the scope of employment, physical or not.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Servant to employee

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Respondeat superior and the line between employees and independent contractors under the Restatement (Second) (§§ 2, 219–220) and the Restatement (Third) (§§ 7.03, 7.07).

Why did the Restatement (Third) drop the term "independent contractor"?
o: Because independent contractors can no longer be agents.
Because it lumped some agents together with non-agent service providers.
Because courts had stopped distinguishing employees from other workers.
Because independent contractors are now treated as employees for all tort purposes.
None of the above.
oe: Some non-employees are agents (an outside lawyer, a broker) and some are not (a builder, a taxi). The R3d keeps both categories.
Correct. The R2d used "independent contractor" as a catch-all. The R3d sorts the workforce into employees, non-employee agents, and non-agent service providers.
Courts still distinguish employees for vicarious-liability purposes.
The general rule remains that a principal is not vicariously liable for a non-employee's physical torts.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Independent contractor

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Respondeat superior and the line between employees and independent contractors under the Restatement (Second) (§§ 2, 219–220) and the Restatement (Third) (§§ 7.03, 7.07).

Which of the following factors from Restatement (Second) § 220(2) tend to show that a worker is a servant (employee)?
o: The employer supplies the tools and the place of work.
The worker is paid by the hour rather than by the job.
The work is part of the employer's regular business.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Supplying instrumentalities and the workplace points toward employment.
True. Payment by time rather than by the job points toward employment.
True. Work within the employer's regular business suggests a servant.
Incomplete. Work in the employer's regular business is also a factor pointing to employment.
Correct. All three § 220 factors point toward a servant relationship. Contract labels are informative but never decisive.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Section 220 factors

q: Three equal partners each contribute $40,000 in cash. In year one the partnership earns $240,000 in profit, allocated equally. Each partner draws $50,000 during the year. What is each partner's capital account at year end?
o: None of the above.
oe: That is only the opening contribution. Profits and draws change the account.
That adds the $80,000 profit share but ignores the $50,000 draw.
Correct. Capital account = contributions + allocated profits − allocated losses − draws: $40,000 + $80,000 − $50,000 = $70,000. The account is kept at book value, not market value.
That adds the draw to the contribution instead of the profit share.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Capital account arithmetic

q: Under UPA § 38(2), when a partner wrongfully dissolves a partnership for a term before the term ends, what may the innocent partners do?
o: Continue the business and pay the wrongdoer the value of their interest, less damages, with goodwill left out of the valuation.
Declare the wrongdoer's entire interest forfeited to the remaining partners.
Nothing; the UPA requires a liquidation sale whenever a partnership dissolves.
Continue the business, but only if they pay the wrongdoer full value including goodwill.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The innocent partners may continue (alone or with others), securing payment of the wrongdoer's interest valued without goodwill and less damages for the breach (Pav-Saver v. Vasso).
The UPA reduces the wrongdoer's payout by damages and goodwill; it does not forfeit the whole interest.
Liquidation is the rule for rightful dissolution (§ 38(1)). After a wrongful dissolution the innocent partners have the option to continue.
Leaving out goodwill is one of the penalties the UPA imposes on the wrongful partner.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — UPA wrongful dissolution

q: A partner in a limited liability partnership negligently injures a client while doing partnership work. Who may be personally liable to the client?
o: Only the LLP, because the shield protects every partner.
The LLP and all of the partners, jointly and severally.
The LLP and the negligent partner only.
Only the negligent partner, because an LLP is never liable for its partners' torts.
None of the above.
oe: The shield protects partners from liability that arises solely from being partners. It does not protect a partner from their own tort.
That is the general-partnership rule. In an LLP, partnership obligations are the LLP's alone (RUPA § 306(c)).
Correct. The LLP is liable for a partner's actionable conduct in the ordinary course (§ 305), and the negligent partner answers for their own tort. The other partners are shielded (§ 306(c)).
The LLP itself is liable for a partner's actionable conduct in the ordinary course of its business.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LLP partner's own tort

q: How does Restatement (Second) § 379 treat the duty of care of a gratuitous agent compared with that of a paid agent?
o: The two owe exactly the same standard.
A paid agent is held to a higher standard than a gratuitous one.
A gratuitous agent owes no duty of care at all.
A gratuitous agent owes a higher standard because no contract limits the duty.
None of the above.
oe: The Restatement distinguishes them.

Correct. A gratuitous agent must use the care required of persons doing similar gratuitous undertakings for others, which is less demanding. The R3d (§ 8.08) also lets the standard vary with whether the agent is paid.
A gratuitous agent still owes care, and the full duty of loyalty.
Being unpaid does not raise the standard.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Gratuitous agent's care

q: Under RUPA § 409(c), which of the following breaches a partner's duty of care?
o: An ordinarily negligent business decision.
Reckless conduct in the partnership's business.
A knowing violation of law.
B and C.
A, B and C.
oe: No. Ordinary negligence is not a breach under § 409(c).
Breach. Grossly negligent or reckless conduct falls below the standard.
Breach. Knowing violations of law are listed in § 409(c).

Correct. The duty of care is to refrain from grossly negligent or reckless conduct, willful or intentional misconduct, and knowing violations of law. Ordinary negligence does not breach it (compare Bane v. Ferguson).
Ordinary negligence is not a breach, so A does not belong.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Care is gross negligence

q: The members of a member-managed LLC vote to make a distribution that leaves the LLC unable to pay its debts as they come due. Under the ULLCA, who is personally liable?
o: No one, because § 304 shields every member.
The members who consented to it, for the excess.
Every member, for all of the LLC's debts, because the distribution pierced the veil automatically.
Only the creditors who were not paid, who must bear the loss.
None of the above.
oe: The shield covers company debts, not a member's own liability for consenting to an improper distribution.

Correct. An LLC may not make a distribution that leaves it insolvent (§ 405). Members or managers who consent to an improper distribution are personally liable to the company for the excess (§ 406), and a person who knowingly received it may also have to return it.
An improper distribution creates a specific liability for the excess; it does not automatically pierce the veil.
The statute protects creditors by making consenting members liable for the excess.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Improper LLC distribution

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Forming a partnership. Apply RUPA § 202 (and UPA §§ 6–7 where a question says so). No question involves a filing with the state.

Must the parties intend to form a partnership for one to exist?
o: Yes. A partnership forms only if each party subjectively intends to be a partner.
Yes, and they must also sign a written partnership agreement.
No. A partnership is formed by what the parties do, whatever they intend.
No, but they must file a statement of partnership authority.
None of the above.
oe: Subjective intent is not required; the test looks at what the parties do.
No writing is needed to form a general partnership.
Correct. RUPA § 202(a) (and UPA § 6) make partnership a status. Parties can form one inadvertently, and a disclaimer does not control if they do the things that make a partnership.
A statement of authority is optional and has nothing to do with formation.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Intent not required

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Forming a partnership. Apply RUPA § 202 (and UPA §§ 6–7 where a question says so). No question involves a filing with the state.

A person who receives a share of a business's profits is presumed to be a partner. Which of the following does NOT rebut that presumption?
o: The profits were paid as wages to an employee.
The profits were paid as interest on a loan, even though the rate varied with profits.
The profits were paid as the price of the goodwill of a business the recipient sold.
The profits were paid to an investor who put capital at risk and shares in control.
None of the above.
oe: This rebuts it. Wages are a listed exception (§ 202(c)(3); Fenwick).
This rebuts it. Interest on a loan is an exception even if it varies with profits.
This rebuts it. Payment for goodwill or other property is a listed exception.
Correct. None of the exceptions fits, and capital at risk plus control are themselves signs of co-ownership (Zajac v. Harris).
D does not rebut the presumption.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Profit-sharing presumption

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Forming a partnership. Apply RUPA § 202 (and UPA §§ 6–7 where a question says so). No question involves a filing with the state.

Which statement about co-ownership of property and sharing of gross returns is correct?
o: Neither, by itself, establishes a partnership; profit sharing is what counts.
Co-owners who share the rent from their building are partners as a matter of law.
Sharing gross returns raises the same presumption of partnership as sharing profits.
Co-ownership of property used in a business always establishes a partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. RUPA § 202(c)(1)–(2) and UPA § 7(2)–(3) say so. Sharing profits, not gross returns, raises the presumption.
Co-ownership and sharing rent do not by themselves make a partnership, whether or not the co-owners share profits from the property.
Only profit sharing raises the presumption.
Co-ownership is a factor, not a test.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Co-ownership and gross returns

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Forming a partnership. Apply RUPA § 202 (and UPA §§ 6–7 where a question says so). No question involves a filing with the state.

How does a joint venture compare with a general partnership?
o: A joint venture must be formed by a filing with the state.
It is a partnership for a limited undertaking, governed by partnership law.
Joint venturers owe each other no fiduciary duties because the venture is temporary.
Joint venturers have limited liability by default.
None of the above.
oe: No filing is needed; a joint venture arises from the parties' agreement and conduct.

Correct. Joint venturers owe each other partners' duties (Meinhard v. Salmon; Sandvick v. LaCrosse). The Sandvick elements are contributions, a proprietary interest and mutual control, an agreement to share profits, and a contract forming it.
Meinhard v. Salmon involved a joint venture and set the highest standard of loyalty.
Like general partners, joint venturers have no default liability shield.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Joint venture

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Forming a partnership. Apply RUPA § 202 (and UPA §§ 6–7 where a question says so). No question involves a filing with the state.

Which of the following facts point toward a partnership rather than an employment or lending relationship?
o: The person contributed capital that is at risk in the business.
The person shares losses as well as profits.
A lender receives a capped share of profits, information rights, and a veto over speculative deals in return for a large loan.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Points toward partnership (Zajac v. Harris).
Points toward partnership (Kaufman-Brown Potato Co. v. Long).
These were reasonable protections for a lender in Martin v. Peyton, which held the lenders were not partners.
Correct. Capital at risk and loss sharing show co-ownership. Lender protections like those in Martin v. Peyton do not, unless together they amount to control of the business.
C describes the protections Martin v. Peyton held were consistent with being a lender.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Facts pointing to partnership

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Apparent authority (R3d §§ 2.03, 3.03; R2d §§ 8, 27, 159) and inherent agency power (R2d §§ 8A, 161, 194–195).

Apparent authority requires a manifestation by whom, and to whom?
o: By the agent, to the third party, in the agent's own words.
By the principal, to the agent.
By the principal, to the third party.
By the third party, to the principal.
None of the above.
oe: The agent's own statements can never by themselves create apparent authority.
A manifestation to the agent is the basis of actual authority.
Correct. Apparent authority exists when a third party reasonably believes the agent has authority and the belief is traceable to the principal's manifestations (R3d § 2.03).
The third party makes no manifestation in this analysis.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Source of manifestation

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Apparent authority (R3d §§ 2.03, 3.03; R2d §§ 8, 27, 159) and inherent agency power (R2d §§ 8A, 161, 194–195).

Which of the following can be a principal's manifestation supporting apparent authority?
o: Placing the agent in a position whose holders customarily have such authority.
The principal's silence when it would be expected to speak.
The agent's own repeated assurances that they are authorized.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. Position is a manifestation (Lind v. Schenley; R3d § 3.03 cmt. b).
True. In Ackerman v. Sobol, the clients' presence and silence at the mediation held their lawyer out.
Not enough on its own. The agent's say-so can bolster reasonableness only once the principal's manifestation exists.
Correct. Position and silence where one would be expected to speak are principal manifestations. The agent's own statements are not.
C cannot create apparent authority.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — What counts as a manifestation

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Apparent authority (R3d §§ 2.03, 3.03; R2d §§ 8, 27, 159) and inherent agency power (R2d §§ 8A, 161, 194–195).

Which statement best distinguishes apparent authority from estoppel?
o: Apparent authority binds both the principal and the third party to the contract; estoppel makes the principal liable for the loss of a third party who detrimentally changed position.
Estoppel binds both parties to the contract, while apparent authority compensates only reliance losses.
The two doctrines are identical and require the same proof.
Estoppel requires an intentional misrepresentation; carelessness is never enough.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Estoppel (R3d § 2.05) protects only a relying third party, who must show a change of position. Apparent authority makes the transaction itself binding on both sides.
This reverses the two doctrines.
Estoppel requires detrimental change of position and can rest on the principal's carelessness; apparent authority requires a manifestation.
Carelessly causing the belief, or failing to correct it, is enough (Hoddeson v. Koos Bros.).
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Apparent authority vs. estoppel

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Apparent authority (R3d §§ 2.03, 3.03; R2d §§ 8, 27, 159) and inherent agency power (R2d §§ 8A, 161, 194–195).

Under Restatement (Second) § 195, the rule applied in Watteau v. Fenwick, an undisclosed principal who puts an agent in charge of a business as its apparent owner is liable for which acts of the agent?
o: None, because the third party never knew the principal existed.
Only acts the principal actually authorized.
Acts usual in such a business, even if the principal forbade them.
Any act at all, even one far outside the kind of business the agent manages.
None of the above.
oe: Watteau held the undisclosed principal liable despite the third party's ignorance.
Liability extends beyond actual authority; the brewers in Watteau had forbidden the cigar purchases.

Correct. This is inherent agency power. The R3d replaces it with § 2.06(2): an undisclosed principal may not rely on instructions that reduce the agent's authority below what a third party would assume if the principal were disclosed.
The rule reaches only acts usual in that kind of business.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal's manager

q: Which of the following statements about kinds of agents are true?
o: A general agent is authorized to conduct a series of transactions involving continuity of service.
A special agent is authorized to conduct a single transaction or a series of transactions without continuity of service.
A subagent is appointed directly by the principal and owes duties only to the agent who supervises them.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True (R2d § 3(1)).
True (R2d § 3(2)).
False. A subagent is appointed by an agent, and the subagent is a fiduciary of the principal as well (R3d §§ 1.04(8), 3.15).
Correct. A and B state the R2d § 3 definitions. C misstates subagency.
C is false.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Kinds of agents

q: Under the majority rule stated in Kerl v. Rasmussen, when is a franchisor vicariously liable for a franchisee's negligence?
o: Whenever the franchisee uses the franchisor's trademark.
When it controls the specific part of the operation that caused the harm.
Whenever the franchisor sets uniform quality standards.
Never, because a franchisee is always an independent business with its own owners.
None of the above.
oe: A trademark license alone does not make the franchisor a principal (Murphy v. Holiday Inns).
Correct. Quality and brand standards are not control. Arby's had no say over hiring or supervision, so it was not liable for the franchisee's negligent supervision.
System-wide quality standards protect the brand and are not control of daily operations.
Pervasive operational control can make a franchisor a principal (Parker v. Domino's; Miller v. McDonald's).
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Franchisor liability

q: Under RUPA § 503, what does a transferee of a partner's transferable interest receive?
o: The transferor's distributions.
The right to participate in management in the transferor's place.
Unlimited access to the partnership's books and records.
Automatic admission as a partner.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A transferee gets only economic rights. The transfer is permitted and does not by itself dissociate the transferor (§ 503(a)–(b)).
A transferee has no management rights.
A transferee generally has no right to information; on dissolution it gets an account only from the date of dissolution (§ 503(c)).
Admission after formation requires the agreement, an Article 11 transaction, or all partners' consent (§ 402(b)).
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Transferee's rights

q: In a two-partner firm, partner X tells a supplier in advance that X objects to a routine purchase. Partner Y makes the purchase anyway. Reading National Biscuit Co. v. Stroud with Summers v. Dooley, which statement is most accurate?
o: The partnership is not bound, because X's objection was communicated to the supplier.
The partnership is bound, and Y may always make the partnership reimburse the cost, because the purchase was in the ordinary course.
Neither the partnership nor Y is bound, because the partners are deadlocked.
The partnership is bound to the supplier, but as between the partners, Y acted without majority approval.
None of the above.
oe: In National Biscuit, Stroud's notice did not help him: as one of two equal partners he was not a majority and could not restrict Freeman.
Summers v. Dooley denied reimbursement for an expense the majority never approved.
Deadlock suspends the power to act internally, but it does not void transactions with third parties.
Correct. As to third parties National Biscuit controls; among the partners Summers controls. Covalt v. High reconciles them: an even split suspends the power to act internally, not as to outsiders.
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — National Biscuit and Summers

q: Which of the following is NOT true of a sole proprietorship?
o: The owner may operate under a trade name.
The owner is personally liable for all of the business's debts.
It is the default form for one person doing business alone.
It is a separate legal entity that shields the owner.
None of the above.
oe: True. A sole proprietor may use a trade name.
True. There is no separation of personal and business liabilities.
True. No filing is needed.
Correct. This is not true. A sole proprietorship is not a separate entity and offers no shield.
D is not true of a sole proprietorship.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Sole proprietorship

q: In Frigidaire Sales Corp. v. Union Properties, limited partners who also ran the LP's corporate general partner were sued personally on the LP's contract. What did the court hold?
o: They were liable as general partners because they controlled the business.
They were not personally liable, because they acted as officers of the corporate general partner and the creditor knew it was dealing with the corporation.
They were liable because a corporate general partner is always undercapitalized as a matter of law.
They were liable only for the LP's tort obligations.
None of the above.
oe: The court rejected the control-rule argument on these facts.
Correct. A corporate general partner gives everyone in the LP limited liability. The court said the remedy for an undercapitalized corporate general partner is veil piercing.
Undercapitalization is a veil-piercing argument that must be proved, not a rule of law.
The case involved a contract claim, and the holding was no personal liability.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Corporate general partner

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissociation under RUPA Article 6. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing on the point.

Which statement about a partner's power to dissociate is true under the RUPA?
o: Every partner has the power to dissociate at any time by express will.
A partner in a term partnership has no power to withdraw before the term ends.
The partnership agreement may take away a partner's power to dissociate.
A partner may dissociate only with the consent of a majority of the partners.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Section 602(a) gives every partner the power to leave (Collins v. Lewis). Whether leaving is rightful is a separate question.
The partner has the power, though using it early may be wrongful.
It may not (§ 105(c)(9)); it may only require the notice of withdrawal to be in a record.
No consent is needed to dissociate by express will.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Power to dissociate

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissociation under RUPA Article 6. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing on the point.

In a partnership for a definite term, which of the following dissociations before the term ends is wrongful?
o: A partner withdraws by express will, and the withdrawal does not follow within 90 days after another partner's death-type or wrongful dissociation.
A partner is expelled by judicial order.
A partner dies.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Wrongful (§ 602(b)(2)(A)).
Wrongful (§ 602(b)(2)(B)).
Not wrongful. Death is not on the § 602(b) list.
Correct. Early withdrawal by express will and judicial expulsion are wrongful in a term partnership; so is becoming a debtor in bankruptcy. Death is not.
Death is not wrongful dissociation.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Wrongful dissociation

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissociation under RUPA Article 6. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing on the point.

Under RUPA § 603, what is the effect of a partner's dissociation?
o: The dissociated partner is released from all partnership debts incurred while they were a partner.
The partnership always dissolves and must wind up.
The partner's management rights end, and so do duties for later matters.
The partner keeps full management rights until the buyout price is paid.
None of the above.
oe: Dissociation does not by itself discharge existing liabilities (§ 603(c)).
The § 603(a) switch sends the case to Article 8 only if a § 801 event occurs; otherwise Article 7's buyout applies.
Correct. Section 603(b) ends management rights and limits the § 409 duties to matters arising before dissociation, except for a partner who participates in winding up.
Management rights end at dissociation.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Effect of dissociation

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissociation under RUPA Article 6. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing on the point.

On application by the partnership or another partner, for which of the following may a court expel a partner under RUPA § 601(5)?
o: Wrongful conduct that adversely and materially affected the partnership's business.
Willful or persistent material breach of the partnership agreement or of a duty under § 409.
Conduct relating to the business that makes it not reasonably practicable to carry on the business in partnership with that partner.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A ground (§ 601(5)(A)).
A ground (§ 601(5)(B)).
A ground (§ 601(5)(C); Giles v. Giles Land Co.).
Incomplete. C is also a ground.
Correct. All three are statutory grounds, and the agreement may not vary them (§ 105(c)(10)).
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Judicial expulsion

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissociation under RUPA Article 6. Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing on the point.

Which of the following may a partnership agreement do?
o: List events that cause a partner's dissociation and allow expulsion by a vote of the other partners.
Change the grounds on which a court may expel a partner.
Require a partner's notice of withdrawal to be in a record.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: Not permitted (§ 105(c)(10)).
Permitted. This is the one change § 105(c)(9) allows to the power to dissociate.
Correct. The agreement may add dissociation events and expulsion procedures and may require written notice of withdrawal, but it may not vary the judicial expulsion grounds.
B is forbidden by § 105(c)(10).
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Agreement and dissociation

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duty of loyalty under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.01–8.06) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 387–396).

An agent uses their position to earn money from a third party. The principal suffered no loss. Must the agent account to the principal?
o: Yes, for any material benefit gained through the position.
No, unless the agent's conduct was also a crime under the law of the place where it occurred.
Only if the agent was paid for their services.
No, because the principal cannot show any damages.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. R3d § 8.02 (and R2d § 388) require it. In Reading v. Regem, the Crown kept the sergeant's bribes even though it lost nothing.
Criminality is not required; it only happened to be present in Reading.
Gratuitous agents owe the same duty of loyalty.
Disgorgement does not depend on loss to the principal.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Profit from position

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duty of loyalty under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.01–8.06) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 387–396).

Under R3d § 8.06, a principal's consent cures conduct that would otherwise breach the duty of loyalty if which of the following is true?
o: The agent acts in good faith and deals fairly with the principal.
The agent discloses all material facts the agent knows or should know would affect the principal's judgment.
The consent covers a specific act or transaction, or acts of a specified type that could reasonably be expected in the ordinary course.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Required.
Required.
Required. Blanket consent to anything does not cure.
Incomplete. The consent must also cover a specific act or type of act.
Correct. Section 8.06 requires good faith, full disclosure of material facts, fair dealing, and consent that is specific to an act or type of act.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Consent that cures

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duty of loyalty under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.01–8.06) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 387–396).

What does General Automotive Manufacturing Co. v. Singer teach about orders a principal seems unable to fill?
o: The agent must disclose them and let the principal decide what to do with them.
The agent may decide for themselves which orders the principal cannot handle and keep the profit on those.
An agent's side business is permitted whenever the principal is working at full capacity.
Only an express non-compete clause limits an agent's side dealings.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Singer secretly sent orders he thought the shop couldn't handle to other shops and kept the markup. As a fiduciary he had to disclose them; he had to disgorge $64,088.
That was Singer's argument, and the court rejected it.
Capacity does not excuse nondisclosure.
The duty of loyalty applies without any contract clause.
A is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Whose opportunity

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duty of loyalty under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.01–8.06) and the Restatement (Second) (§§ 387–396).

After an agency ends, and with no non-compete agreement, which of the following may the former agent do?
o: Compete with the former principal.
Use the general skill and knowledge acquired during the agency.
Use the former principal's written customer list, which qualifies as a trade secret.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Permitted. The duty not to compete ends with the agency.
Permitted (R2d § 396).
Not permitted (Town & Country v. Newbery; R3d § 8.05).
Correct. A former agent may compete using general knowledge and skill, but may not use trade secrets or confidential information such as a protected customer list.
C is not permitted.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — After the agency ends

q: In winding up under RUPA § 806, in what order are the partnership's assets applied?
o: Outside creditors; then partners' loans; then partners' capital; then profits.
Creditors, including partners who are creditors; then unreturned contributions; then any surplus in proportion to distribution shares.
Partners' capital first, so that partners recover their investment before creditors are paid.
Partners' loans first, because partners took the greatest risk.
None of the above.
oe: That is the UPA § 40(b) order, which ranks partners' loans behind outside creditors.

Correct. RUPA § 806 pays partner-creditors together with outside creditors, then returns contributions, then splits the surplus. Partners contribute to cover any shortfall on obligations incurred while the firm was not an LLP.
Creditors are always paid before partners get back their capital.
Neither act puts partner loans ahead of outside creditors.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — RUPA § 806 order

q: Under RUPA § 401(k), which of the following require the consent of all partners by default?
o: An act outside the ordinary course of the partnership's business.
An amendment to the partnership agreement.
An ordinary-course purchase of inventory.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Requires unanimity.
Requires unanimity.
A majority decides ordinary-course matters.
Correct. Ordinary matters go by majority; acts outside the ordinary course and amendments to the agreement need everyone (UPA § 18(h) adds acts that contravene the agreement).
Ordinary-course matters need only a majority.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Unanimity by default

q: Under Kovacik v. Reed, when one partner contributes all of the money and the other contributes only services, and the venture loses the capital, what happens?
o: The service partner must pay the money partner half of the lost capital.
Losses are shared in proportion to each partner's capital contribution.
Each partner loses their own contribution, money or labor.
The money partner may recover all of the lost capital from the service partner.
None of the above.
oe: That is the statutory result under UPA § 18(a), which Kovacik declined to apply.
Kovacik did not adopt a capital-ratio rule; the service partner contributed no capital.
Correct. The court held that the party who contributed money may not recover any part of it from the party who contributed only services.
Nothing supports making the service partner bear all of the money loss.
C is correct.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Kovacik rule

q: Under ULLCA § 701(a)(4), on a member's application, on which grounds may a court dissolve an LLC?
o: The conduct of all or substantially all of the company's activities is unlawful.
It is not reasonably practicable to carry on the company's activities in conformity with the certificate of organization and the operating agreement.
Those in control of the company have acted in a manner that is oppressive and directly harmful to the applicant.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A ground.
A ground.
A ground. In an oppression case the court may order a remedy other than dissolution (§ 701(b)).
Incomplete. Oppression by those in control is also a ground.
Correct. All three are grounds, and the operating agreement may not vary them (§ 105). Oppression is a ground that RUPA § 801(4) does not list.
topic: 14 · LLCs — LLC judicial dissolution

q: A principal keeps an agent on staff knowing the agent has a history of assaulting customers. The agent assaults a customer for purely personal reasons, outside the scope of employment. On what basis may the principal be liable?
o: On no basis, because the assault was outside the scope of employment.
Only if the principal later ratifies the assault.
Directly, for its own negligent retention of the agent.
Only if the principal intended the assault.
None of the above.
oe: Scope matters only for vicarious liability. Direct liability rests on the principal's own fault.
Ratification is one route to direct liability, but not the only one.
Correct. A principal is directly liable when its own negligence in selecting, training, retaining, supervising, or controlling an agent causes the harm. No scope-of-employment finding is needed.
Intent is one route under R2d § 219(2), but negligence or recklessness is enough.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Negligent retention

q: Under RUPA § 308, to whom is a purported partner liable?
o: To a person who relies on the representation in dealing with the firm.
To anyone who deals with the firm, whether or not they knew of the representation.
Only to persons who signed the partnership agreement.
To anyone, whenever the person is named as a partner in a filed statement of partnership authority.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. And if the representation was made in a public manner, the purported partner is liable to anyone who relies on it, even without knowing they were held out to that claimant. Reliance is essential (Young v. Jones).
Liability requires reliance on the representation.
Purported-partner liability runs to outsiders, not to signers of the agreement.
Being named in a statement of authority does not by itself make a person liable as a partner (§ 308(c)).
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Purported partner

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissolution under the UPA (1914). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the UPA with no agreement on the point.

Under the UPA, which of the following causes dissolution of a partnership?
o: In an at-will partnership, a partner's express will to dissolve.
The death of any partner.
The admission of a new partner.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Causes dissolution (§ 31(1)(b)).
Causes dissolution (§ 31(4)).
Does not. Adding a partner never dissolved a UPA partnership.
Correct. Under the UPA's aggregate theory, any partner's departure dissolves the partnership; adding a partner does not.
Admitting a partner does not dissolve the firm.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — UPA dissolution events

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissolution under the UPA (1914). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the UPA with no agreement on the point.

A partner in a UPA partnership formed for a five-year term announces in year two that they are leaving. What is the result?
o: No dissolution, because the partner had no power to leave before the term ended.
Dissolution, but a wrongful one, with the UPA § 38(2) consequences.
Rightful dissolution, because any partner may leave at any time.
No dissolution until a court orders it.
None of the above.
oe: Under the UPA, partners always have the power to dissolve; the agreement cannot take it away.
Correct. The partner had the power but not the right. The innocent partners may continue the business and pay the wrongdoer's interest less damages, without goodwill.
Leaving early breaches the term, so the dissolution is wrongful.
Dissolution happens on the partner's express will; a court order is one route, not a requirement.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Leaving a UPA term partnership

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissolution under the UPA (1914). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the UPA with no agreement on the point.

Which of the following is NOT true of a UPA partnership after dissolution?
o: The partnership is not terminated but continues until winding up is complete (§ 30).
Partners' authority is generally limited to acts needed to wind up the business (§ 33).
Partners' fiduciary duties end the moment dissolution occurs.
A partner may still bind the firm to some third parties who lack notice of the dissolution (§ 35).
None of the above.
oe: True.
True.
Correct. This is not true. Duties continue through winding up (Monin v. Monin; Second Measure v. Kim).
True. The UPA's notice and advertising rules protect such third parties.
C is not true.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — After UPA dissolution

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissolution under the UPA (1914). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the UPA with no agreement on the point.

After a rightful dissolution under UPA § 38(1), absent an agreement otherwise, what may any partner insist on?
o: A liquidation: sale of the assets and payment in cash.
That the others continue the business without paying the departing partner anything.
That the others buy them out at going-concern value.
That the other partners be expelled.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. This liquidation right is why UPA dissolution was so destabilizing; RUPA replaced it with buyouts for many departures, and Creel v. Lilly refused to force a fire sale.
The departing partner is entitled to their share.
Going-concern buyouts are a RUPA § 701 concept.
Dissolution gives no such right.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Rightful dissolution

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Dissolution under the UPA (1914). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a general partnership governed by the UPA with no agreement on the point.

Under UPA § 40(b), in what order are partnership liabilities paid on liquidation?
o: Partners' capital, then outside creditors, then partners' loans, then profits.
Outside creditors and partners' loans together, then capital, then profits.
Profits first, then capital, then creditors.
Outside creditors, partner loans, capital, then profits.
None of the above.
oe: Creditors always come before partners' capital.
Treating partner-creditors equally with outsiders is the RUPA § 806 approach.
Creditors come first under both acts.
Correct. The UPA ranks partner loans behind outsiders but ahead of capital. Partners then contribute to cover shortfalls in proportion to their loss shares (§ 40(d); In re Fulton).
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — UPA § 40 order

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Ratification (R3d §§ 4.01–4.08; R2d § 82) and estoppel (R3d § 2.05; R2d § 8B).

Which of the following are requirements for ratification?
o: The principal knows, or has reason to know, the material facts.
The principal affirms the entire transaction.
The act was done, or purported to be done, on the principal's behalf.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Required (R3d § 4.06; Ercanbrack).
Required. There is no partial ratification (§ 4.07).
Required (§ 4.03; Botticello v. Stefanovicz).
Incomplete. The act must also have been done or purported to be done on the principal's behalf.
Correct. Ratification also requires capacity, and it can be express or implied, most often by accepting benefits.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification requirements

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Ratification (R3d §§ 4.01–4.08; R2d § 82) and estoppel (R3d § 2.05; R2d § 8B).

When can a principal's silence ratify an unauthorized act?
o: Never; ratification must be express.
Whenever the principal fails to object within a reasonable time, whether or not it knew of the act.
When the principal knows of the transaction and stays silent where it would be expected to object.
Only if the third party has already performed.
None of the above.
oe: Ratification can be implied, including by silence.
Knowledge is required. "Ratification of an act about which the principal knows nothing is inherently impossible" (Ercanbrack).
Correct. Silence can be a manifestation of assent if the principal has knowledge of the material facts and a reasonable person would have spoken up.
The third party's performance is not the test.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ratification by silence

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Ratification (R3d §§ 4.01–4.08; R2d § 82) and estoppel (R3d § 2.05; R2d § 8B).

Which statement correctly contrasts the Restatements on ratification by an undisclosed principal?
o: The R2d allows only disclosed and unidentified principals to ratify; the R3d allows any principal, including an undisclosed one.
Both Restatements allow any principal to ratify.
The R2d allows any principal to ratify; the R3d allows only disclosed principals.
Neither Restatement allows an unidentified principal to ratify.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The R2d required that the agent have purported to act for the principal. The R3d drops the limit for undisclosed principals.
The R2d did not let an undisclosed principal ratify.
This reverses the rule.
Both allow unidentified (partially disclosed) principals to ratify.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal ratification

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Ratification (R3d §§ 4.01–4.08; R2d § 82) and estoppel (R3d § 2.05; R2d § 8B).

Which of the following does NOT prevent ratification?
o: The third party withdrew from the transaction before the principal ratified.
A material change in circumstances would make it inequitable to bind the third party.
The principal learned the material facts only after the act, but before ratifying.
Performance of the contract had become illegal when the principal tried to ratify.
None of the above.
oe: This prevents ratification (R3d § 4.05).
This prevents ratification (§ 4.05).
Correct. Knowledge is required when the principal ratifies, not when the agent acts.
This prevents ratification.
C does not prevent ratification.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Limits on ratification

q: A contract says the worker is "an independent consultant and not an agent." In practice the worker runs daily operations and signs checks. What is the effect of the label?
o: It is conclusive, because the parties are free to define their relationship.
It is not controlling; the actual relationship decides.
It creates an agency only if both parties sign it.
It shifts the burden of proving agency to the worker.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control the legal characterization.
Correct. R3d § 1.02 says the parties' labels do not control. MJ & Partners v. Zadikoff held that a "consultant" who ran the restaurant could be an agent owing loyalty.
Signing has no bearing on whether the label controls.
The party asserting agency bears the burden either way.
B is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Labels don't control

q: Which statement about a general partner of an ordinary limited partnership is true?
o: The general partner is personally liable unless the LP is an LLLP.
The general partner's liability is limited to their capital contribution.
The general partner has no management rights.
The general partner owes no fiduciary duties to the LP.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In an LP only the limited partners are shielded. The LLLP form (or a corporate general partner, as in Frigidaire) extends protection to the general partner.
That describes limited partners.
The general partner is the one who manages.
General partners owe fiduciary duties, though Delaware lets the agreement displace them (Sonet; El Paso).
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — General partner of an LP

q: In Meinhard v. Salmon, what did Chief Judge Cardozo hold that Salmon owed Meinhard regarding the new lease?
o: Nothing, because the joint venture was about to end.
The entire new lease, because Meinhard had financed the original venture.
Damages for competing with the hotel during the lease term.
Disclosure of the opportunity, so Meinhard could compete for it.
None of the above.
oe: That was the dissent's view.
Meinhard received a half interest, not the whole lease.
The issue was the taken opportunity, not competition with the hotel.
Correct. As manager and co-venturer, Salmon owed "the punctilio of an honor the most sensitive." The deal was an extension of the venture, so Meinhard was entitled to share in it.
D is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Meinhard's duty

q: In a RUPA partnership at will, a partner gives notice of their express will to withdraw. What is the result?
o: Dissociation only; the others continue and buy out the partner under Article 7.
Nothing happens until a court approves the withdrawal.
The partnership is dissolved and its business must be wound up (§ 801(1)).
A wrongful dissociation that makes the partner liable for damages.
None of the above.
oe: In an at-will partnership, express will to withdraw is a § 801(1) dissolution event, so the § 603 switch goes to Article 8.
No court approval is needed.

Correct. In an at-will partnership a partner's express will to withdraw causes both dissociation and dissolution. (The partners may still agree to continue the business, but the default is winding up.)
Withdrawal from an at-will partnership is rightful unless it breaches an express term.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — At-will withdrawal

q: Which pairings of buyout trigger and funding source are standard planning tools?
o: Death, funded by life insurance.
Disability, funded by disability insurance.
Retirement, funded by a pension or 401(k).
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Standard.
Standard.
Standard.
Incomplete. Retirement is matched with pension or 401(k) funding.
Correct. Each trigger is matched with a funding source; otherwise the agreement uses a price formula and payment terms.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Funding buyouts

q: An agent signs a contract on behalf of a principal without any authority. The principal refuses to ratify, and the third party did not know the agent lacked authority. What is the agent's liability?
o: None, because the agent signed only as an agent.
The agent is liable for breach of the implied warranty of authority, including the benefit the third party expected, unless the agent disclaimed it.
Only if the agent committed fraud.
The agent automatically becomes the principal on the contract in every case.
None of the above.
oe: Signing as an agent does not protect someone who had no power to bind the principal.

Correct. Under R3d § 6.10, one who purports to bind a principal without power is liable for the third party's loss unless the principal ratifies, the agent disclaims, or the third party knew the agent lacked authority.
No fraud is needed; the warranty is implied.
An agent becomes a party when the principal is undisclosed, unidentified, or nonexistent, not in every case of missing authority.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Implied warranty of authority

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partnership property and partners' transferable interests under RUPA §§ 203–204 and 501–504, compared with the UPA where a question says so.

Property is bought with partnership funds but titled in a partner's own name, with no indication of the partner's capacity or of the partnership. How is it treated under RUPA § 204?
o: It is presumed to be partnership property.
It is conclusively the partner's separate property, because title controls.
It is presumed to be the partner's separate property.
It is owned by the partners as tenants in common.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Purchase with partnership assets raises the presumption, even without the partnership's name on the title (§ 204(c)).
Title is important but not conclusive; use of partnership funds creates a presumption the other way.
That presumption applies only when the partner's own funds were used and nothing indicates the partnership (§ 204(d)).
Neither act uses tenancy in common for this property.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Partnership funds, partner's name

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partnership property and partners' transferable interests under RUPA §§ 203–204 and 501–504, compared with the UPA where a question says so.

Property is titled in a partner's own name, bought with the partner's own money, and used in the partnership's business. Nothing in the title indicates the partnership. How is it treated under RUPA § 204(d)?
