o: It is presumed to be partnership property because the partnership uses it.
It is presumed to be the partner's separate property.
It is conclusively partnership property.
It is owned half by the partner and half by the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Use by the partnership does not by itself create a presumption of partnership ownership.
Correct. Section 204(d) presumes separate property in these circumstances. Intent at acquisition still controls, and partners should agree in writing which assets the firm owns.
No presumption is conclusive under § 204.
There is no such split rule.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Partner's own funds

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partnership property and partners' transferable interests under RUPA §§ 203–204 and 501–504, compared with the UPA where a question says so.

A partner's personal judgment creditor wants to reach the partner's interest in the partnership. What may the creditor obtain under RUPA § 504?
o: A levy on specific partnership property, such as the firm's truck.
Admission as a partner in place of the debtor.
A charging order on the partner's distributions.
The right to vote the partner's share in management decisions.
None of the above.
oe: A partner has no interest in specific partnership property that can be reached (§ 501).
A creditor never becomes a partner by collecting a debt.
Correct. The charging order reaches distributions only. The creditor gets no management or voting rights, and the order does not dissociate the partner.
A charging order carries no voting rights.
C is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Charging order

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partnership property and partners' transferable interests under RUPA §§ 203–204 and 501–504, compared with the UPA where a question says so.

In Putnam v. Shoaf, a partner sold her entire partnership interest. Later the partnership recovered money from banks over a bookkeeper's embezzlement. What result, and why?
o: She shared in the recovery, because the embezzlement occurred while she was a partner.
She shared in the recovery, because she remained co-owner of the partnership's specific claims.
The sale was void because it dissolved the partnership.
She received nothing; selling her entire interest passed everything, including claims unknown at the time of sale.
None of the above.
oe: The court rejected that view.
A partner owns an interest in the partnership, not specific assets or claims.
The sale was valid.
Correct. The claims belonged to the partnership, and she had sold her whole interest in it.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Selling the whole interest

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partnership property and partners' transferable interests under RUPA §§ 203–204 and 501–504, compared with the UPA where a question says so.

Which of the following bear on whether property is partnership property?
o: Whether title is in the partnership's name or indicates a partner's capacity or the partnership.
Whether partnership funds were used to acquire it.
The partners' intent when the property was acquired.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Relevant (§ 204(a)–(b)).
Relevant (§ 204(c)).
Relevant. Intent at acquisition controls (In re Fulton).
Incomplete. Intent at acquisition also matters.
Correct. Title, source of funds, and intent at acquisition all matter. In re Fulton found a trailer bought with a partner's borrowed money but titled to the business was partnership property.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — What decides ownership

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Scope of employment under Restatement (Second) §§ 228–231 and Restatement (Third) § 7.07.

Which of the following is NOT an element of Restatement (Second) § 228's scope-of-employment test?
o: The conduct is of the kind the servant is employed to perform.
It occurs substantially within the authorized time and space limits.
It is actuated, at least in part, by a purpose to serve the master.
The master earned a profit from the specific act.
None of the above.
oe: An element (§ 228(1)(a)).
An element (§ 228(1)(b)).
An element (§ 228(1)(c)).
Correct. This is not an element. A purpose to serve the master is required, not an actual benefit to the master.
D is not an element.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — R2d § 228 elements

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Scope of employment under Restatement (Second) §§ 228–231 and Restatement (Third) § 7.07.

Under Restatement (Third) § 7.07, when is an employee's act outside the scope of employment?
o: When it occurs outside working hours.
When it serves no purpose of the employer at all.
Whenever it violates a rule the employer has announced to its employees.
Whenever it is an intentional tort.
None of the above.
oe: Time is not the R3d test. The R3d fixed the R2d's time-and-space prong, which fit poorly for professionals.
Correct. Otherwise, an employee acts within scope when performing assigned work or engaging in a course of conduct subject to the employer's control.
Forbidden acts can still be within scope.
Intentional torts can be within scope.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — R3d § 7.07

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Scope of employment under Restatement (Second) §§ 228–231 and Restatement (Third) § 7.07.

Which of the following statements about scope of employment are true?
o: An act the employer forbade can still be within the scope of employment.
Intentional torts are always outside the scope of employment.
A serious crime is usually outside the scope of employment.
A and C.
A, B and C.
oe: True (R2d § 230).
False. Manning v. Grimsley and Lamkin v. Brooks put intentional torts within scope.
True. Seriously criminal acts usually signal a departure.
Correct. Forbidden acts may be within scope; serious crimes usually are not. Intentional torts can go either way.
B is false.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Forbidden acts and crimes

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Scope of employment under Restatement (Second) §§ 228–231 and Restatement (Third) § 7.07.

Why did Judge Friendly hold the government liable in Ira S. Bushey & Sons v. United States?
o: Because the risk was characteristic of the enterprise.
Because the sailor was trying to serve the Coast Guard when he turned the wheels.
Because the government ratified the sailor's conduct.
Because the government was negligent in hiring the sailor.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Friendly used an enterprise-risk test instead of the R2d motive test. Sailors' drinking on shore leave and crossing the drydock were foreseeable risks. A purely personal act would not have been.
The court accepted that the sailor had no purpose to serve his employer.
There was no ratification.
The case was decided on respondeat superior, not negligent hiring.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Bushey's rationale

q: A principal is generally not liable for the torts of an independent contractor. Which of the following is NOT an exception to that rule?
o: The principal retained control over the contractor's work.
The principal negligently selected an incompetent contractor.
The work was inherently dangerous unless special precautions were taken.
The principal owed a nondelegable duty that the contractor's work was meant to perform.
None of the above.
oe: An exception. Retained control can make the principal liable.
An exception, based on the principal's own negligence.
An exception (Majestic Realty v. Toti Contracting).
An exception (Kleeman v. Rheingold).
Correct. All four are recognized exceptions, along with abnormally dangerous activities, which carry strict liability.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Independent contractor exceptions

q: An agent deposits money collected for the principal into the agent's personal bank account. Nothing is lost. Which duty has the agent breached?
o: The duty of care.
The duty to account.
The duty of obedience.
The duty to provide information.
None of the above.
oe: Care concerns how competently the agent performs, not how the principal's property is held.
Correct. The agent must keep the principal's property separate, keep and render accounts, and not make it appear to be the agent's own (R2d §§ 382, 398). No loss is needed for a breach.
Obedience is breached by disobeying lawful instructions, and none were given here.
Disclosure concerns facts the principal would want to know.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Commingling

q: In Fenwick v. Unemployment Compensation Commission, a receptionist and her employer signed a "partnership agreement" giving her 20% of profits. How did the court classify her?
o: As a partner, because the signed agreement said so.
As a partner by estoppel, because customers thought she was a partner.
As an employee whose profit share was really a wage.
As a joint venturer for a single undertaking.
None of the above.
oe: Labels do not control.
No one relied on a representation of partnership; the issue was unemployment-tax coverage.

Correct. Weighing intent, profit and loss sharing, ownership and control, conduct toward others, and rights on dissolution, the court found no co-ownership. The wages exception defeats the profit-sharing presumption.
Nothing about a single undertaking was involved.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Fenwick's receptionist

q: Under RUPA § 702, for how long may a dissociated partner still bind a continuing partnership to a third party who does not know or have notice of the dissociation and reasonably believes the person is still a partner?
o: 90 days.
One year.
Two years.
Indefinitely, until the partnership dissolves.
None of the above.
oe: Ninety days is how long after filing a statement of dissociation before third parties are deemed to have notice (§ 103(d)), which cuts the power off sooner.
The statute uses two years.

Correct. The partnership is bound if the act would have bound it under § 301 before dissociation, less than two years have passed, and the third party lacks knowledge or notice and reasonably believes the person is a partner.
The power is limited to two years.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Lingering power after dissociation

q: What is a limited liability limited partnership (LLLP)?
o: An LP that has filed to shield its general partners too.
An LLP that has added members who manage it.
An LLC that has elected to be taxed as a partnership.
A limited partnership in which the limited partners manage the business.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. In an ordinary LP the general partner has unlimited liability; an LLLP extends the shield to the general partners. It requires a filing.
An LLP has only general partners; it does not have members.
An LLC is a different entity; its tax treatment does not make it an LLLP.
The general partners manage an LLLP, just as in an LP.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LLLP

q: An agent tells a seller that the agent is buying for a company but does not say which company. Under the Restatement (Third) and Atlantic Salmon v. Curran, is the agent personally liable on the contract?
o: Yes, as a party to the contract.
Only if the seller could not have found the principal's identity through public records.
Only if the principal turns out to be insolvent.
No, because the agent disclosed that they were acting as an agent.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under R3d § 6.02 both the agent and, once identified, the principal are bound. Curran owed about $255,000 personally.
Atlantic Salmon held that the seller's ability to search public records does not matter; the burden of disclosure is on the agent.
The principal's solvency does not change whether the agent is a party.
Disclosing the agency is not enough; the agent must disclose the principal's identity to avoid being a party.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Unidentified principal

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' management rights and authority to bind the partnership under RUPA §§ 301, 303, 401, and 410. Assume no statement of partnership authority has been filed unless a question says otherwise.

Under RUPA § 301(1), a partner's act apparently carrying on in the ordinary course the partnership's business binds the partnership unless which of the following is true?
o: The partner lacked authority and the third party knew or had notice of it.
The partner lacked authority for the act, whether or not the third party knew it.
The other partners objected after the transaction was made.
The act cost more than the partnership's average monthly expenses.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Both conditions are needed. Without knowledge or notice, the partnership is bound even though the partner exceeded actual authority (RNR Investments).
Lack of authority alone is not enough; the third party must also have known or had notice.
Objections after the fact do not undo the partnership's liability.
There is no dollar threshold in § 301.
A is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Section 301 apparent authority

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' management rights and authority to bind the partnership under RUPA §§ 301, 303, 401, and 410. Assume no statement of partnership authority has been filed unless a question says otherwise.

Under RUPA § 301(2), when does a partner's act that is NOT apparently in the ordinary course of the partnership's business bind the partnership?
o: When a majority of the partners approved it.
When the third party acted in good faith.
Never, under any circumstances.
When the other partners authorized it.
None of the above.
oe: A majority suffices for ordinary-course matters, not for acts outside the ordinary course.
Good faith alone does not make an extraordinary act binding.
Such an act binds the partnership if the other partners authorized it.
Correct. Acts outside the ordinary course bind the firm only with the other partners' authorization, which matches the internal rule that such acts need unanimity (§ 401(k)).
D is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Outside the ordinary course

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' management rights and authority to bind the partnership under RUPA §§ 301, 303, 401, and 410. Assume no statement of partnership authority has been filed unless a question says otherwise.

Must a lender read the partnership agreement before making a loan arranged by one partner?
o: Yes, a lender is charged with knowing every term of the agreement.
No; absent knowledge or notice, it has no duty to inquire.
Yes, for any loan over the amount fixed in the statute.
Only if a statement of partnership authority has been filed.
None of the above.
oe: There is no such rule.
Correct. In RNR Investments v. Peoples First Community Bank, the bank that did not know of a cap on the general partner's borrowing could enforce the $990,000 loan.
The RUPA sets no dollar threshold.
A filed limit is generally not notice anyway, except for real property transfers.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — No duty to read the agreement

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' management rights and authority to bind the partnership under RUPA §§ 301, 303, 401, and 410. Assume no statement of partnership authority has been filed unless a question says otherwise.

Partner P contributed 90% of a partnership's capital and partner Q contributed 10%. Their agreement is silent on management and profits. Which statement is correct by default?
o: P has 90% of the vote on management decisions.
P may veto any decision because P contributed most of the capital.
P and Q have equal management rights and equal shares of profits.
Profits are split 90/10, but votes are equal.
None of the above.
oe: Votes are not weighted by capital.
No partner has a default veto over ordinary matters.

Correct. Each partner has equal rights in management (§ 401(h)) and an equal share of distributions (§ 401(a)), regardless of capital contributed. The unequal capital is returned first in winding up (§ 806(b)).
Profit shares are also equal by default.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Equality regardless of capital

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' management rights and authority to bind the partnership under RUPA §§ 301, 303, 401, and 410. Assume no statement of partnership authority has been filed unless a question says otherwise.

Which of the following statements are true under the RUPA?
o: A partner who binds the partnership through apparent authority while exceeding actual authority may be liable to the partnership for the resulting loss.
The partnership must indemnify a partner for liabilities the partner incurred in the ordinary course of the partnership's business.
The partnership may recover from a partner whose ordinary negligence in partnership work caused it tort liability.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True. The partnership may sue a partner for breach of the agreement or a duty (§ 410(a)).
True (§ 401(c); Moren v. Jax Restaurant).
False. Moren held that the statute gives partners indemnity from the partnership, not the reverse, for ordinary-course negligence.
Correct. The firm bears ordinary-course liabilities, but a partner who overrides limits on actual authority may answer to the firm.
C misstates Moren.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Indemnity and claims among partners

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Managing an LLC under ULLCA § 407, and who owes duties under § 409. Unless a question says otherwise, assume the operating agreement is silent.

Under ULLCA § 407(a), when is an LLC manager-managed?
o: Only when the operating agreement expressly says it is manager-managed, managed by managers, or that management is vested in managers, or uses words of similar import.
Whenever it has more than ten members.
Whenever the certificate of organization names a person as manager.
Whenever a majority of members vote to hire a manager.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Otherwise the LLC is member-managed.
The number of members does not matter.
Under § 407 the operating agreement decides, not the certificate.
Hiring someone to run operations does not by itself change the LLC's management structure.
A is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Default management

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Managing an LLC under ULLCA § 407, and who owes duties under § 409. Unless a question says otherwise, assume the operating agreement is silent.

In a manager-managed LLC, which of the following require the consent of all members?
o: An act outside the ordinary course of the company's activities.
An amendment to the operating agreement.
An ordinary-course decision about the company's activities.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Requires all members (§ 407(c)(3)(A)).
Requires all members (§ 407(c)(3)(B)).
Decided by the manager, or a majority of managers (§ 407(c)(1)).
Correct. Even in a manager-managed LLC, extraordinary acts and amendments need every member's consent.
Ordinary matters belong to the managers.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Unanimity in a manager-managed LLC

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Managing an LLC under ULLCA § 407, and who owes duties under § 409. Unless a question says otherwise, assume the operating agreement is silent.

In a manager-managed LLC, how may a manager be removed by default?
o: Only for cause, by unanimous vote of the members.
By a majority of members, without cause.
Only by court order on a member's application.
Only by the other managers.
None of the above.
oe: The default is easier than that.
Correct (§ 407(c)(4)). A manager is also chosen by a majority of the members, and a manager need not be a member.
No court is needed.
The members, not the other managers, remove a manager.
B is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Removing a manager

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Managing an LLC under ULLCA § 407, and who owes duties under § 409. Unless a question says otherwise, assume the operating agreement is silent.

In a manager-managed LLC, who owes the fiduciary duties of loyalty and care?
o: The members and the managers equally.
The members only, because they own the company.
The managers alone.
No one, because an LLC is a creature of contract.
None of the above.
oe: Members of a manager-managed LLC do not owe those duties solely by being members.
The managers, who run the company, owe the duties.
Correct (§ 409(i)). In a member-managed LLC, by contrast, the members owe loyalty and care.
The ULLCA imposes duties that the operating agreement may modify but not eliminate.
C is correct.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Who owes duties

q: Under A. Gay Jenson Farms Co. v. Cargill, when does a creditor become the principal of its debtor?
o: Whenever it lends the debtor money.
Whenever it takes a security interest in the debtor's assets.
When it takes de facto control of the debtor's business.
Whenever it buys most of the debtor's products.
None of the above.
oe: Lending alone does not create agency (compare Martin v. Peyton).
Security interests are ordinary protections for a lender.
Correct. Cargill approved major decisions, audited, criticized daily, and supplied forms. A creditor that takes over management becomes a principal (R2d § 14O) and inherits the debtor's obligations.
A buyer is not a principal just because it buys most of the output (R2d § 14K).
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Creditor as principal

q: Under Restatement (Second) § 161, a general agent of a disclosed principal can bind the principal to which acts?
o: Acts usually incidental to authorized transactions, even if forbidden, if the third party reasonably believes the agent is authorized and has no notice otherwise.
Any act at all, whatever the third party believes.
Only acts the agent was actually authorized to do.
Only acts the principal represented to the third party as authorized.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. This is inherent agency power for disclosed principals (Kidd v. Thomas A. Edison; Nogales Service Center). No manifestation by the principal is needed.
The third party must reasonably believe the agent is authorized.
Section 161 reaches beyond actual authority.
That describes apparent authority, which § 161 supplements.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — R2d § 161

q: Which statement about the LLC is correct?
o: An LLC is a kind of corporation.
It pairs limited liability with pass-through taxation.
Each member is personally liable for the torts of the other members.
An LLC must have at least two members.
None of the above.
oe: LLCs are not corporations.
Correct. LLCs are creatures of contract. The main exception to the shield is veil piercing.
Members are not liable for company obligations solely because they are members (ULLCA § 304).
An LLC may have one or more members.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — What an LLC is

q: Which statement correctly compares an incoming partner's liability for partnership debts incurred before the partner joined?
o: Under both acts, the incoming partner is fully and personally liable for those debts.
Under both acts, the incoming partner has no exposure at all, and even partnership property cannot be used to pay those debts.
Under the UPA, the incoming partner is not liable; under the RUPA, they are personally liable.
Under UPA § 17, the incoming partner is liable for prior debts but only out of partnership property; under RUPA § 306(b), they are not personally liable for them.
None of the above.
oe: Neither act imposes full personal liability on an incoming partner for prior debts.
Partnership property remains available to pay the partnership's debts.
This reverses the rule, and overstates both.
Correct. Under both acts the incoming partner's personal assets are safe from pre-admission debts, but their stake in the partnership is at risk.
D is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Incoming partner

q: When do courts decline to apply the Kovacik v. Reed rule?
o: When the service partner was paid a salary.
When the service partner made any capital contribution, even a nominal one.
When the RUPA governs, because the RUPA rejects Kovacik.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Kovacik is not applied in that case.
Kovacik is not applied in that case.
The RUPA's comment says the default loss rules apply even if a partner contributed no capital.
Incomplete. The RUPA also rejects the rule.
Correct. Kovacik is a narrow exception to the default rule that losses follow profits.
topic: 11 · Loss sharing (Kovacik) — Limits of Kovacik

q: In Kleeman v. Rheingold, a lawyer hired a process server who botched service, and the client's claim was lost. What did the court hold?
o: The lawyer was not liable, because the server was an independent contractor.
The lawyer could be liable, because the duty to serve process is nondelegable.
The lawyer was liable only if negligent in choosing the server.
The lawyer was liable only if the lawyer supervised the server.
None of the above.
oe: The independent-contractor rule gave way to the nondelegable duty.
Correct. Some duties are so important that hiring an independent contractor does not shift responsibility (R3d § 7.06).
Liability did not depend on negligent selection.
Supervision was not required.
B is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Nondelegable duty

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' fiduciary duties under RUPA § 409 and the limits on changing them in § 105. Unless a question says otherwise, the partnership agreement says nothing about duties.

Under RUPA § 409(e), does a partner violate a duty just because their conduct furthers their own interest?
o: No, not solely for that reason.
Yes, always; a partner must act solely for the partnership.
Yes, unless a court approves the conduct in advance.
Yes, unless the partner gives up their interest in the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Partners may pursue their own interests, as long as they meet the specific duties of loyalty and care and act in good faith.
That overstates the partner's duty. Partners are co-owners with their own stakes.
No court approval is needed.
Nothing requires that.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Furthering one's own interest

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' fiduciary duties under RUPA § 409 and the limits on changing them in § 105. Unless a question says otherwise, the partnership agreement says nothing about duties.

A partner wants to sell a building to the partnership. Which of the following statements are true under RUPA § 409?
o: All the partners may authorize or ratify the sale after full disclosure of all material facts.
It is a defense to an adverse-dealing claim that the transaction was fair to the partnership.
A majority of the partners may ratify the sale without any disclosure.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. Ratification requires all partners and full disclosure, unless the agreement provides another method.
Correct. Adverse dealing can be cured by informed unanimous approval, and fairness is a defense.
C is false.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Adverse dealing

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' fiduciary duties under RUPA § 409 and the limits on changing them in § 105. Unless a question says otherwise, the partnership agreement says nothing about duties.

Under RUPA § 105, which of the following MAY a partnership agreement do?
o: Eliminate the duty of loyalty entirely.
Relieve a partner of liability for intentional misconduct.
List activities that do not violate loyalty, if not manifestly unreasonable.
Eliminate the obligation of good faith and fair dealing, if the partners all agree in writing.
None of the above.
oe: Not permitted (§ 105(c)(5)).
Not permitted (§ 105(c)(8)).
Correct. The agreement may also alter aspects of loyalty, alter care, and set procedures for disinterested approval, all if not manifestly unreasonable.
Not permitted (§ 105(c)(6)), though the agreement may set reasonable standards for measuring it.
C is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — What the agreement may do

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' fiduciary duties under RUPA § 409 and the limits on changing them in § 105. Unless a question says otherwise, the partnership agreement says nothing about duties.

In Bane v. Ferguson, a retired partner sued the managing partners after a bad merger ended his pension. What did the court hold?
o: The managing partners owed him the same duties they owed current partners.
Duties run to current partners, not former ones.
The managing partners were strictly liable for the firm's collapse.
The retired partner could sue only the partnership's creditors.
None of the above.
oe: The court held the opposite.
Correct. Judge Posner also relied on the business judgment rule. The case shows who is owed partner duties and how low the duty of care is.
No strict liability applies to business decisions.
Creditors were not the issue.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Former partners

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' fiduciary duties under RUPA § 409 and the limits on changing them in § 105. Unless a question says otherwise, the partnership agreement says nothing about duties.

A family oil partnership's agreement expressly lets partners compete with the partnership for their own accounts. Two partners buy a parcel the family had discussed buying. Following Singer v. Singer, did they breach a duty?
o: Yes, because Meinhard v. Salmon always controls.
No; the clause permitted it.
Yes, unless they paid the partnership fair value for the parcel.
Yes, because the family had discussed the parcel.
None of the above.
oe: Meinhard states the default; the agreement changed it.
Correct. Partners can contract around the duty not to take opportunities (today, if not manifestly unreasonable, § 105(d)).
Nothing required payment.
The clause covered even opportunities the partnership had considered.
B is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Contracting around opportunities

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited partnerships. Unless a question says otherwise, assume an LP formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) whose agreement says nothing on the point.

How is a limited partnership formed?
o: By filing a certificate of limited partnership with the state.
By a written agreement naming the general and limited partners.
By registering the business's trade name.
By the limited partners' payment of their capital contributions.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Without a filed certificate, the parties are likely general partners, and the would-be limited partners lose the shield.
An agreement alone forms only a general partnership.
Registering a trade name does not create an LP.
Contributions do not form the entity.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Forming an LP

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited partnerships. Unless a question says otherwise, assume an LP formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) whose agreement says nothing on the point.

Which of the following is NOT a default right of a limited partner?
o: The right to share in distributions.
The right to information about the LP's activities and records.
Binding the LP as its agent.
The right to sue a general partner for breach of fiduciary duty.
None of the above.
oe: A limited partner shares in profits and distributions.
Limited partners have information rights, although more limited than a general partner's.
Correct. This is not a right of a limited partner. A limited partner is not an agent of the LP solely by being a limited partner, and the general partner manages.
Limited partners may sue general partners, directly or derivatively.
C is not a limited partner's right.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Limited partner's rights

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited partnerships. Unless a question says otherwise, assume an LP formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) whose agreement says nothing on the point.

How do Delaware courts treat an LP agreement that clearly replaces default fiduciary duties with contract standards?
o: They refuse to enforce it, because fiduciary duties are mandatory.
They enforce it only if a court approved the agreement in advance.
They apply default fiduciary duties anyway, because the investors are passive.
They enforce it as written.
None of the above.
oe: Delaware lets the agreement displace default fiduciary duties.
No court approval is needed.
Investors' passivity does not override a clear agreement.
Correct. In Sonet v. Plum Creek the agreement sent investors to "the ballot box, not the courthouse," and in El Paso a conflicts committee's subjective good faith was the standard.
D is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Delaware's contract-first approach

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited partnerships. Unless a question says otherwise, assume an LP formed under the Uniform Limited Partnership Act (ULPA) (2001) whose agreement says nothing on the point.

In Jerman v. O'Leary, the LP agreement let the general partners buy partnership land in their "sole discretion." What did the court hold?
o: The clause eliminated all of the general partners' duties regarding the purchase.
It allowed the purchase but still required fair value and disclosure.
The purchase was void, because general partners can never buy partnership property.
The purchase required a unanimous vote of the limited partners.
None of the above.
oe: The court did not read the clause that broadly.
Correct. Their appraisal ignored a favorable rezoning. Courts may read fiduciary duties into permissive clauses (contrast Delaware's approach in Sonet).
The clause allowed the purchase.
The case turned on fair value and disclosure, not a vote.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Permissive clause

q: What principle does Rose v. Giamatti illustrate?
o: One can be an agent for some purposes but not others.
The Commissioner was MLB's agent for every purpose, because MLB appointed him.
Agency requires a written contract between principal and agent.
Arbitrators are always agents of the parties who appoint them.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The clubs had given the Commissioner exclusive, independent disciplinary authority they could not control, like an arbitrator, so he was not MLB's agent for discipline.
Appointment alone did not make him an agent for discipline.
No writing is required to create agency.
The court reasoned the opposite: independent authority is inconsistent with agency.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Agent for some purposes

q: Which of the following does a principal owe an agent by default?
o: Reimbursement of expenses the agent properly incurs within the scope of actual authority.
Indemnity for losses the agent suffers in carrying out the principal's instructions.
A fiduciary duty of loyalty to the agent.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Owed (R3d § 8.14).
Owed (R3d § 8.14).
Not owed. The principal's duties are contractual, plus good faith and fair dealing (§ 8.15); the agent is the fiduciary.
Correct. A principal also owes compensation if it was agreed or contemplated, cooperation, and warnings about known risks.
The principal does not owe the agent loyalty.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Principal's default duties

q: In Clackamas Gastroenterology Associates v. Wells, what decided whether the clinic's physician-owners counted as employees under the ADA?
o: Their titles as shareholders and directors.
The common-law control test.
Whether they owned any shares at all.
The number of hours they worked each week.
None of the above.
oe: The Court said titles do not decide the question.

Correct. The factors include hiring and firing, supervision, reporting to someone higher, influence over the organization, the parties' intent, and sharing in profits, losses, and liabilities. Owners who run the business are employers, not employees.
Share ownership is part of the picture, not the test.
Hours worked is not the standard.
B is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Owners as employees

q: What does Day v. Sidley & Austin illustrate?
o: Every partner has a statutory veto over any merger.
Partners must disclose every internal change before any vote.
Partners can contract around statutory defaults.
A partner who loses a title may force dissolution of the firm.
None of the above.
oe: The agreement in Day let a majority approve the merger.
The court held the fiduciary duty did not require disclosing changes that brought no profit to the others or loss to the firm.
Correct. The agreement gave an executive committee control of firm policy. Day lost his sole chairmanship but had no claim.
No such right exists.
C is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Contracting around defaults

q: Which of the following is a recognized disadvantage of the general partnership?
o: Two layers of income tax.
An elaborate state filing to form it.
Partners cannot act as agents of the firm.
Unlimited liability and limited life.
None of the above.
oe: General partnerships have a single, pass-through layer of tax.
No filing is needed.
Every partner is an agent of the partnership.
Correct. The listed cons also include conflict among partners and problems with expansion, succession, and termination. The pros are simplicity, one layer of tax, and pooled resources.
D is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Drawbacks of a general partnership

q: Under RUPA § 901(b), what vote is needed for a general partnership to become an LLP?
o: A simple majority of the partners.
The vote needed to amend the partnership agreement, which by default is unanimity (or, if the agreement addresses contribution obligations, the vote needed to amend those terms).
Two-thirds of the partners by capital.
No vote; any partner may file the statement of qualification.
None of the above.
oe: The statute ties the vote to amending the agreement, not a simple majority.
Correct. Because the shield changes partners' obligations to contribute, the act requires the amendment-level vote before the statement of qualification is filed.
No two-thirds rule appears in § 901.
The filing comes only after the required approval.
B is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Vote to become an LLP

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: A partner's dissociation when the business continues: RUPA Article 7 (§§ 701–704). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing about buyouts.

Under RUPA § 701(b), how is a dissociated partner's buyout price determined?
o: As the amount that would have been distributable if, on the date of dissociation, the assets were sold at the greater of liquidation value or going-concern value without the partner.
As the book balance of the partner's capital account.
As fair market value on the date of payment.
As liquidation value only.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The partnership then subtracts damages for wrongful dissociation and other amounts the partner owes, and adds interest from the date of dissociation.
Book value applies only if the agreement says so (as in G & S v. Belman).
Value is fixed as of the dissociation date.
The partner gets the greater of liquidation and going-concern value.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Buyout price

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: A partner's dissociation when the business continues: RUPA Article 7 (§§ 701–704). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing about buyouts.

Which of the following statements about the RUPA § 701 buyout price are true?
o: Interest accrues on the price from the date of dissociation.
Damages for wrongful dissociation are offset against the price.
Goodwill is excluded from the valuation when the partner dissociated wrongfully.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. The goodwill penalty was a UPA § 38(2) rule; RUPA has no goodwill deduction.
Correct. The price carries interest, and damages and other amounts owed are subtracted. There is no goodwill penalty.
C states the UPA rule, not the RUPA rule.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Adjustments to the buyout

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: A partner's dissociation when the business continues: RUPA Article 7 (§§ 701–704). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing about buyouts.

Under RUPA § 701(e), if no agreement on the buyout price is reached within 120 days after a written demand for payment, what must the partnership do?
o: Dissolve and wind up its business.
Nothing; the dissociated partner loses the right to be bought out.
Pay its estimate of the price, with interest.
Wait for a court to set the price before paying anything.
None of the above.
oe: The failure to agree does not cause dissolution.
The right is not lost.
Correct. The partnership must tender its estimate; a partner who disagrees may sue within 120 days after the tender to have a court fix the price.
The partnership must pay its estimate first.
C is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — 120 days

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: A partner's dissociation when the business continues: RUPA Article 7 (§§ 701–704). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing about buyouts.

A partner wrongfully dissociates before the end of a definite term. When is the partner entitled to payment of the buyout price under RUPA § 701(h)?
o: Immediately, like any other dissociated partner.
Not until the term ends, absent a showing of no undue hardship.
Never; a wrongful dissociator forfeits the whole buyout price to the remaining partners.
Only after forcing a liquidation of the partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Wrongful dissociators from term partnerships must generally wait.
Correct. A deferred payment must be adequately secured and bear interest.
There is no forfeiture; damages are offset instead.
A wrongful dissociator cannot force a liquidation.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Wrongful dissociator's wait

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: A partner's dissociation when the business continues: RUPA Article 7 (§§ 701–704). Unless a question says otherwise, assume a partnership governed by the RUPA whose agreement says nothing about buyouts.

Which of the following statements are true under RUPA §§ 703–704?
o: A dissociated partner is generally not liable for partnership obligations incurred after dissociation.
A dissociated partner may be liable, for up to two years, on a transaction with a third party who lacks notice of the dissociation and reasonably believes the person is still a partner.
Filing a statement of dissociation gives third parties constructive notice after 90 days, cutting off that lingering liability and power to bind.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Incomplete. The statement of dissociation also matters.
Correct. The two-year exposure ends sooner once a filed statement has been effective for 90 days. Dissociation never releases the partner from obligations incurred before leaving (§ 603(c)).
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Liability after leaving

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Disclosed, unidentified (partially disclosed), and undisclosed principals under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 6.01–6.04) and the Restatement (Second) (§ 4).

When is a principal "undisclosed"?
o: When the third party knows the agent acts for a principal but does not know who the principal is.
When the third party knows both that the agent acts for a principal and who the principal is.
When the third party has no notice that the agent is acting for a principal at all.
When the principal does not exist.
None of the above.
oe: That is an unidentified (partially disclosed) principal.
That is a disclosed principal.
Correct. The third party thinks the agent is the only party to the deal (R3d § 1.04(2)(b)).
That is the § 6.04 problem of a nonexistent principal.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal defined

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Disclosed, unidentified (partially disclosed), and undisclosed principals under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 6.01–6.04) and the Restatement (Second) (§ 4).

An agent acting with actual authority makes a contract on behalf of a disclosed principal. Who are the parties to the contract?
o: The principal and third party.
Only the agent.
Neither, until the principal ratifies.
The agent and the principal, jointly.
None of the above.
oe: Correct (R3d § 6.01). Disclosing both the agency and the principal's identity protects the agent.
The disclosed principal is a party.
Ratification is needed only if the agent lacked authority.
The agent is not a party unless they agree to be.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Disclosed principal

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Disclosed, unidentified (partially disclosed), and undisclosed principals under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 6.01–6.04) and the Restatement (Second) (§ 4).

An agent for an undisclosed principal makes a contract within actual authority. Which statements are true?
o: The agent is a party to the contract.
The principal is also a party once discovered, and must indemnify the agent.
The third party cannot enforce the contract against the principal, because the third party never relied on the principal.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True (R3d § 6.03).
True. The third party can enforce against the principal once identified, unless the contract excludes it.
False. Reliance on the principal is not required.
Correct. Both the agent and the undisclosed principal are bound.
C is false.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Undisclosed principal's contract

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Disclosed, unidentified (partially disclosed), and undisclosed principals under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 6.01–6.04) and the Restatement (Second) (§ 4).

An agent signs a contract for a corporation that has not yet been formed. Under R3d § 6.04, who is bound?
o: The agent, unless the agent and third party agreed otherwise.
No one, because there is no principal.
Only the corporation, automatically, once it is formed.
The third party bears the loss for failing to check whether the corporation existed.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A person who acts for a principal that does not exist or lacks capacity is a party to the contract.
The agent is bound.
A later-formed entity is not automatically bound.
The burden is on the agent, as in Atlantic Salmon v. Curran.
A is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Nonexistent principal

q: In Gorton v. Doty, why was the coach the teacher's agent when he drove her car to the game?
o: She paid him to drive.
Her condition that he drive gave consent and control.
They signed a written agreement making him her agent for the trip to the game.
The school directed him to drive her car.
None of the above.
oe: He was not paid; agency needs no compensation.
Correct. A gratuitous favor with one condition supplied consent and control, making her liable for his driving.
There was no written agreement.
The court focused on her manifestation, not the school's.
B is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Gorton's favor

q: In Lind v. Schenley Industries, why was the company bound to Kaufman's promise of a 1% commission?
o: Kaufman had actual authority to set salesmen's pay.
Lind relied on Kaufman's own statements that he could set pay.
It held Kaufman out as Lind's boss on pay.
The company ratified the promise by paying commissions.
None of the above.
oe: Only the president could set pay; Kaufman lacked actual authority.
An agent's own statements cannot create apparent authority.
Correct. The vice president sent Lind to Kaufman about salary. The principal's manifestation through the position it gave Kaufman made Lind's belief reasonable.
The case rested on apparent (and inherent) authority, not ratification.
C is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Lind's commission

q: Under Restatement (Second) § 267, as applied in Williams v. Dimensions Health Corp., a hospital may be vicariously liable for an independent-contractor surgeon if which of the following is shown?
o: The hospital held itself out as providing the care, as through its trauma center.
The patient relied on the hospital, looking to the facility rather than to a particular doctor.
The patient's reliance was reasonable.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Required: a representation.
Required: reliance.
Required: reasonableness. A disclaimer buried in an unsigned form did not defeat it.
Incomplete. The reliance must also be reasonable.
Correct. Representation, reliance, and reasonableness make an apparent agent's tort the principal's.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Hospital apparent agency

q: In Meehan v. Shaughnessy, how did the departing partners breach their duty of loyalty?
o: They unfairly acquired client consents: they denied their plans when asked, prepared client letters in advance, and raced to sign up clients when they gave notice.
They planned to leave and lined up space for a new firm.
They left the firm at all.
They took their personal belongings and desk files.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. They had to prove that clients would have come anyway or hold the profits from those cases in trust for the old firm.
Preparing to leave was not a breach.
Partners may leave; the problem was how they took clients.
That was not the basis of the breach.
A is correct.
topic: 9 · Partners’ fiduciary duties — Grabbing and leaving

q: In a buyout agreement, what does a "shotgun" clause do?
o: It requires an independent appraisal to set the price.
It sets the price at book value.
It forces liquidation of the business on any partner's departure.
One owner names a price; the other must buy or sell at it.
None of the above.
oe: That is an appraisal clause.
That is a book-value formula.
A shotgun clause avoids liquidation.
Correct. The first mover sets the price, which encourages a fair offer, since the offeror may end up on either side.
D is correct.
topic: 12 · Buyout agreements — Shotgun clause

q: Which of the following statements are true under ULLCA §§ 502–503?
o: A transferee of a member's transferable interest receives distributions but has no right to manage.
A charging order is the exclusive remedy by which a member's judgment creditor may satisfy the judgment from the member's transferable interest.
A member's personal judgment creditor may levy on the LLC's own assets to satisfy the debt.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: False. The LLC's assets belong to the entity and are shielded from members' personal creditors.
Correct. The creditor reaches only distributions through a charging order. (For a single-member LLC, a court may order foreclosure, and the buyer takes the whole interest.)
C is false.

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Winding up: distributing a partnership's assets and requiring partners to contribute. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP unless a question says otherwise.

After all creditors are paid, $30,000 remains. Partner X contributed $20,000 and partner Y contributed $4,000, none of which has been returned. They share profits equally. Under RUPA § 806(b), how is the $30,000 distributed?
o: $15,000 to each partner.
$25,000 to X and $5,000 to Y, in proportion to capital.
None of the above.
oe: Unreturned contributions are paid first, before any equal split.
Correct. First X gets back $20,000 and Y $4,000. The remaining $6,000 is split by distribution shares, $3,000 each. X receives $23,000 and Y $7,000.
The surplus is split by distribution shares, which are equal by default, not by capital.
This does not follow the § 806(b) order.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Capital before profits

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Winding up: distributing a partnership's assets and requiring partners to contribute. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP unless a question says otherwise.

A general partnership's assets cannot pay all its creditors. Under RUPA § 806(c), what happens?
o: Each person who was a partner when an unpaid obligation was incurred must contribute, in proportion to their share of distributions, and the others make up any partner's default.
The creditors simply absorb the loss.
Only the managing partner must pay the shortfall.
Partners contribute equally, whatever their profit shares.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Losses follow profit shares, and a partner who pays extra may recover from the partner who defaulted (§ 806(d)).
General partners must contribute to pay partnership creditors.
All partners at the time the obligation was incurred must contribute.
Contributions follow distribution shares, which are equal only by default.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Contribution for shortfalls

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Winding up: distributing a partnership's assets and requiring partners to contribute. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP unless a question says otherwise.

How does RUPA § 806(c) treat an unpaid obligation that was incurred while the partnership was an LLP?
o: Partners must contribute to pay it just as for any other obligation.
Partners must contribute double their usual share.
No contribution is required for LLP-era obligations.
Partners must contribute only for tort obligations.
None of the above.
oe: That would defeat the LLP shield.
There is no such rule.
Correct. The shield works indirectly as well as directly (§ 306(c): no liability "by way of contribution or otherwise").
The current shield covers all LLP obligations.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — LLP-era shortfalls

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Winding up: distributing a partnership's assets and requiring partners to contribute. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP unless a question says otherwise.

Kovacik contributed $10,000; Reed contributed only labor; they agreed to split profits equally. The venture lost $8,680. Under the statutory rule (UPA § 18(a)), rather than the court's holding, what would Reed have owed Kovacik?
o: Nothing.
None of the above.
oe: That is the court's actual holding, not the statutory result.
That would make Reed bear the whole loss.
The loss was $8,680, not $10,000.
Correct. Under the statute losses follow profits, so each bears half of $8,680. Kovacik would get back $1,320 plus Reed's $4,340, or $5,660. The court instead held Reed owed nothing.
D is correct.

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Winding up: distributing a partnership's assets and requiring partners to contribute. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP unless a question says otherwise.

During winding up under RUPA § 804, a partner's act binds the partnership if it is which of the following?
o: Appropriate for winding up the partnership's business.
An act that would have bound the partnership before dissolution, if the other party does not know or have notice of the dissolution.
New business that the other party knows is outside the winding up.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Binding.
Binding.
Not binding. A partner who knowingly binds the firm to new business is liable to the others (§ 805).
Correct. After dissolution, actual authority covers only winding up, but apparent authority can linger until a statement of dissolution has been effective for 90 days.
C is not binding.

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited liability partnerships under RUPA Article 9 and § 306(c), as printed in the supplement.

What is a limited liability partnership?
o: A general partnership that has filed a statement of qualification, so that its partners are shielded from partnership obligations incurred while it is an LLP.
A limited partnership with both general and limited partners.
A corporation owned by partners.
An LLC whose members call themselves partners.
None of the above.
oe: Correct (RUPA §§ 901, 306(c)). It remains a general partnership: all partners manage equally by default.
That is an LP.
An LLP is not a corporation.
An LLC is a different statute and entity.
A is correct.

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited liability partnerships under RUPA Article 9 and § 306(c), as printed in the supplement.

Under the RUPA as printed in the supplement, what does the LLP shield cover?
o: Only tort obligations, as under the earliest LLP statutes.
All LLP-era obligations, contract or tort.
Only contract obligations.
Only obligations above the firm's insurance coverage.
None of the above.
oe: Early statutes had a partial (tort-only) shield; the current act does not.
Correct. A partner is not personally liable for them "solely by reason of being or acting as a partner" (§ 306(c)). A partner still answers for their own wrongful conduct.
The shield is not limited to contracts.
The shield is not tied to insurance.
B is correct.

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited liability partnerships under RUPA Article 9 and § 306(c), as printed in the supplement.

A general partnership owes debts it incurred before filing its statement of qualification. After it becomes an LLP, are the partners shielded from those older debts?
o: Yes, the shield applies retroactively to every existing debt.
Yes, but only if the creditors consent.
No; the shield covers only debts incurred as an LLP.
No, and they also lose the shield for future debts.
None of the above.
oe: The shield covers obligations incurred while the firm is an LLP.
Creditor consent could release partners, but that is not the shield.
Correct. Section 306(c) looks at when the obligation was incurred.
Pre-filing debts do not affect the shield for later debts.
C is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Debts from before the filing

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Limited liability partnerships under RUPA Article 9 and § 306(c), as printed in the supplement.

Which of the following statements about LLPs are true under the RUPA?
o: An LLP's failure to observe formalities is not a ground for imposing liability on a partner for its obligations.
Cancellation of the statement of qualification does not remove the shield for obligations incurred while it was in effect.
An LLP may make a distribution even if it would leave the LLP unable to pay its debts as they come due.
A and B.
A, B and C.

q: Which of the following is a way an agency-type liability arises by operation of law rather than by the parties' own acts?
o: An express agreement between principal and agent.
An agreement implied from the parties' conduct.
Ratification by the principal.
Estoppel.
None of the above.
oe: An express agreement is an act of the parties.
An implied agreement is still an act of the parties.
Ratification is the principal's own act of affirmance.

q: Under R3d §§ 5.03–5.04, an agent's knowledge of a material fact is generally imputed to the principal. When is it NOT imputed?
o: When the agent acts adversely to the principal, for the agent's own or another's purposes, unless imputation is needed to protect a good-faith third party or the principal ratified or kept the benefit.
When the agent learned the fact outside working hours.
When the agent forgot to tell the principal.
When the principal had no actual knowledge of the fact.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The adverse-interest exception reflects the fact that an agent who is working against the principal cannot be expected to pass the information on.
When or where the agent learned the fact does not control if it is material to the agent's duties.
Imputation exists precisely because agents do not always pass information on.
Imputation applies exactly when the principal lacks actual knowledge.
A is correct.

q: Which statement accurately describes how a corporation is governed?
o: Shareholders manage the business day to day.
Shareholders elect directors, who appoint officers.
The officers elect the directors, who answer to the officers.
Directors are personally liable for the corporation's debts.
None of the above.
oe: Shareholders elect directors; they do not manage.

This reverses the chain of authority.
Limited liability protects directors and shareholders alike.
B is correct.

q: What did Page v. Page hold?

At-will partners may dissolve, but only in good faith.
Dissolution required a court order.
None of the above.
oe: A mere hope of profits does not create a term.

An at-will partner may dissolve by express will.
C is correct.

q: Which of the following are purposes of a buyout agreement?
o: An orderly transfer of a departing owner's interest.
Keeping control and choosing who the new owners will be.
Creating a market for the interests of inactive owners.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A purpose.
A purpose.

Correct. Buyout agreements also help pass a family business to the right family members.

q: When a member dissociates from an LLC under the ULLCA, what happens to the member's economic interest by default?

The member keeps it only as a transferee.
The LLC dissolves so that the member can be paid.
The member forfeits it to the other members.
None of the above.

A member's dissociation does not dissolve the LLC.
Nothing is forfeited.
B is correct.

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' personal liability to partnership creditors under RUPA §§ 305–307. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP.

The creditor must get the partner's consent.
None of the above.
oe: Joint and several liability is subject to the exhaustion rule.
Partners may be joined or sued separately (§ 307(b)).

Consent is one way to waive exhaustion, not the general requirement.

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' personal liability to partnership creditors under RUPA §§ 305–307. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP.

What is the effect of a judgment against the partnership alone?
o: It is not by itself a judgment against any partner, and it cannot be satisfied from a partner's assets unless there is also a judgment against that partner.

It is void unless every partner was named.
It lets the creditor seize any partner's home immediately.
None of the above.
oe: Correct (§ 307(c)). The entity and its partners are separate defendants.
Partners must be separately named and adjudged liable.

The partner agreed that the creditor need not exhaust partnership assets.
A court finds that partnership assets are clearly insufficient to satisfy the judgment.
A and B.

Excuses exhaustion (§ 307(d)(3)).

Q7–11 FOCUS: Partners' personal liability to partnership creditors under RUPA §§ 305–307. Assume a general partnership that is not an LLP.

In the ordinary course or with the firm's authority.

None of the above.

Correct. Moren v. Jax Restaurant applied this to a partner's negligence in the kitchen, even though she was partly attending to a personal matter.

That describes a limited partner, not a general partner.
