oe: True (§ 108(b)). A general partnership, by contrast, must carry on a business for profit.
Incomplete. Perpetual duration is also a default.
Correct. Each feature contrasts with the default general partnership: entity status (also RUPA), nonprofit purposes allowed, and perpetual life.
topic: 14 · LLCs — Nature of an LLC

q: In Ackerman v. Sobol Family Partnership, why was the settlement negotiated by the plaintiffs' lawyer enforceable against them?
o: Hiring a lawyer automatically gives the lawyer apparent authority to settle.
The clients' own conduct held the lawyer out: they attended the mediation, conferred with him during the final talks, and never limited his authority.
The lawyer's repeated assurances to defense counsel were enough by themselves.
The clients ratified the settlement by staying silent afterward.
None of the above.
oe: The court said retaining a lawyer, by itself, is not enough.
Correct. Apparent authority can come from the principal's conduct and silence, and it binds even if the agent misread his instructions.
The agent's statements alone never create apparent authority, though they helped show reasonableness here.
The case was decided on apparent authority.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Ackerman's settlement

q: In Brill v. Davajon, a cab driver, against company rules, pushed a stalled car for $1 and caused a collision. Why was the cab company not liable?
o: Because pushing cars was forbidden, and forbidden acts are always outside scope.
Because the driver was an independent contractor.
Because the $1 errand was outside the scope of employment.
Because the collision happened off the company's premises.
None of the above.
oe: Forbidden acts can be within scope (R2d § 230); the rule violation was not the key.
The case turned on scope of employment.
Correct. A personal side errand breaks scope under the purpose prong of R2d § 228 (contrast Bushey).
Cab drivers work off the premises; location was not the issue.
C is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Brill's detour

q: In Bancroft-Whitney Co. v. Glen, which of the president's acts, done while still in office, breached his duty of loyalty?
o: Misleading his employer about a competitor's raid on its staff.
Giving the competitor salary information about the employer's staff.
Choosing which of the employer's editors the competitor should hire and what to offer them.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A breach.
A breach.
A breach.
Incomplete. Choosing whom to hire and what to offer was also a breach.
Correct. Preparing to compete is allowed, but the nature of the preparations matters. The competitor that cooperated was liable too.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Bancroft-Whitney

q: Which development made LLCs practical by letting them combine limited liability with pass-through taxation?
o: IRS pass-through treatment for limited-liability entities.
The abolition of the corporate income tax by Congress in the 1980s.
Every state's adoption of the UPA (1914).
A federal law requiring partnerships to register.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Together with mass financial torts against lawyers and accountants, the savings and loan crisis, and soaring insurance premiums, this drove the spread of LLCs and LLPs.
The corporate income tax was not abolished.
The UPA did not create limited-liability entities.
No such law drove the trend.
A is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Pass-through for limited liability

q: By default, is a partner entitled to pay for services to the partnership?
o: Yes, reasonable compensation for all services.
No, except for services in winding up.
Yes, if the partner's capital contribution was small.
Only the managing partner is entitled to pay.
None of the above.
oe: Partners share profits instead of drawing salaries by default.
Correct (RUPA § 401(j); UPA § 18(f) gave it only to a surviving partner). This default is part of why Kovacik's service partner received nothing for his labor.
Capital has nothing to do with it.
No partner is entitled to pay by default.
B is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Pay for services

q: What did Judge Posner's opinion in EEOC v. Sidley Austin Brown & Wood suggest?
o: State-law partners might be employees if they lack control.
Anyone called a partner is automatically outside federal antidiscrimination law.
Partners who share profits are always employees.
The EEOC may never investigate a law firm.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. A self-perpetuating executive committee controlled the firm, so the 32 demoted partners might be employees despite sharing profits and having capital at risk.
Formal status does not end the inquiry.
Sharing profits points toward partnership, not employment.
The court let the EEOC pursue its subpoena.
A is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — Partners as employees

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Defaults and the partnership agreement. Under RUPA § 105, most of the act's rules are defaults that the partners may change by agreement; § 105(c) lists the rules they may not change.

Which of the following may a partnership agreement NOT do?
o: Change the default rule that profits are shared equally.
Require a unanimous vote for ordinary business decisions.
Vary the grounds for judicial dissolution.
Allow a majority to amend the agreement.
None of the above.
oe: Permitted. Profit shares are a default.
Permitted. The majority rule is a default.
Correct. This is forbidden (§ 105(c)(11)). Partners cannot contract away judicial dissolution, or a transferee's right to seek it under § 801(5).
Permitted. The unanimity rule for amendments is a default.
C is forbidden.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — What the agreement may not change

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Defaults and the partnership agreement. Under RUPA § 105, most of the act's rules are defaults that the partners may change by agreement; § 105(c) lists the rules they may not change.

Which of the following MAY a partnership agreement do?
o: Unreasonably restrict a partner's right to information under § 408.
Relieve a partner of liability for bad-faith conduct.
Change the § 307 rules on suits against partners and exhaustion.
Adopt its own formula for pricing a dissociated partner's buyout.
None of the above.
oe: Forbidden (§ 105(c)(4)).
Forbidden (§ 105(c)(8)).
Forbidden (§ 105(c)(3)). The exhaustion rule protects third parties.
Correct. The § 701 buyout is a default; agreements commonly set their own price (Frank; G & S v. Belman).
D is permitted.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Changing the buyout

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Defaults and the partnership agreement. Under RUPA § 105, most of the act's rules are defaults that the partners may change by agreement; § 105(c) lists the rules they may not change.

A partnership agreement says, "This partnership may never be dissolved." What is the effect under the RUPA?
o: Partners lose the power to dissociate.

The agreement may make the partnership nearly indissoluble by limiting the § 801(1)–(3) events, but it cannot prevent court-ordered dissolution under § 801(4)–(5) or take away the power to dissociate.
The clause is void in its entirety.
The clause converts the partnership into one for a 99-year term.
None of the above.
oe: The power to dissociate cannot be varied (§ 105(c)(9)).
Correct. RUPA makes almost everything a default, which lets partners build a very stable firm, but a few protections are mandatory.
The clause is enforceable to the extent the act allows.
No statute supplies such a term.
B is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — An "indissoluble" partnership

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Defaults and the partnership agreement. Under RUPA § 105, most of the act's rules are defaults that the partners may change by agreement; § 105(c) lists the rules they may not change.

In Frank v. R.A. Pickens & Son Co., partners in a farming partnership bought in at book value, understanding that the manager could end anyone's interest at will and pay book value. When the manager ended Frank's interest, what result?
o: The agreement controlled; he got book value.
Frank could force a liquidation of the whole partnership.
Frank was entitled to fair market value, not book value.
Frank was never a partner, so he received nothing.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Frank was a partner, but UPA rules are defaults that partners can change by agreement.
The agreement displaced the default liquidation right.
The court enforced the book-value term.
The court held he was a partner.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — Frank v. Pickens

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Defaults and the partnership agreement. Under RUPA § 105, most of the act's rules are defaults that the partners may change by agreement; § 105(c) lists the rules they may not change.

Which of the following may a partnership agreement do regarding management?
o: Vest control of firm policy in an executive committee instead of all partners equally.
Weight partners' votes by their capital contributions.
Unreasonably restrict a partner's right to sue the partnership or other partners under § 410(b).
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Permitted (Day v. Sidley & Austin).
Permitted. Equal management rights are a default.
Forbidden (§ 105(c)(7)).
Correct. Equality is only a default; partners may adopt committee management or weighted voting. They may not unreasonably restrict partners' rights to sue.
C is forbidden.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Restructuring management

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Creating an agency relationship: the definition in R3d § 1.01, the terms in R3d §§ 1.03–1.04 and R2d § 3, and subagency (R3d § 3.15).

Which statement about coagents and subagents is correct?
o: A subagent owes no duties to the principal, only to the agent who appointed them.
Coagents are two or more agents of the same principal.
An agent may never appoint a subagent.
Coagents are each other's agents.
None of the above.
oe: A subagent is a fiduciary of the principal as well.
Correct (R3d § 1.04(1)). Coagents are not agents of each other.
An agent with actual or apparent authority to do so may appoint one.
Coagents each act for the principal, not for each other.
B is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Coagents and subagents

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Creating an agency relationship: the definition in R3d § 1.01, the terms in R3d §§ 1.03–1.04 and R2d § 3, and subagency (R3d § 3.15).

What is required for an agent to appoint a subagent whose acts bind the principal, under R3d § 3.15?
o: Authority to appoint the subagent.
Nothing; any agent may appoint any subagent.
The principal must sign the appointment.
The subagent must be an employee of the principal.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The agent remains responsible to the principal for the subagent's conduct, and the subagent acts for both the appointing agent and the principal.
Authority to appoint is required.
The principal need not sign; the agent's authority suffices.
A subagent is appointed by the agent, not employed by the principal.
A is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Appointing a subagent

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Creating an agency relationship: the definition in R3d § 1.01, the terms in R3d §§ 1.03–1.04 and R2d § 3, and subagency (R3d § 3.15).

Who has the burden of proving that an agency relationship exists, and how may it be proven?
o: The party denying agency must disprove it.
The party asserting agency must prove it, but only by a writing.
The party asserting it, by any evidence, even circumstantial.
Agency is presumed between family members.
None of the above.
oe: The burden is on the party asserting agency.
No writing is needed.
Correct. Cargill's agency was proven from the course of dealing between Cargill and Warren.
No presumption arises from family ties (Botticello).
C is correct.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Proving agency

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: Creating an agency relationship: the definition in R3d § 1.01, the terms in R3d §§ 1.03–1.04 and R2d § 3, and subagency (R3d § 3.15).

Under R3d § 1.03, which of the following statements about a manifestation are true?
o: A manifestation may consist of words or conduct.
A manifestation may be made to the agent or to a third party.
A manifestation must be in writing.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True.
True. A manifestation to the agent supports actual authority; one to a third party supports apparent authority.
False.
Correct. A person manifests assent or intention through written or spoken words or other conduct.
C is false.
topic: 1 · Creating the agency relationship — Manifestation

q: In Trustees of the American Federation of Musicians Pension Fund v. Steven Scott Enterprises, why was the fund bound to all 15 settlements its trustee signed?
o: The trustee had actual authority to settle for the fund.
Apparent authority and estoppel bound it until the employer learned of the board's exclusive power, and the fund ratified by cashing all 15 checks with knowledge.
Only ratification applied, because there was never any apparent authority.
The fund was not bound, because the trustee lacked actual authority.
None of the above.
oe: Only the fund's board could settle.
Correct. One fact pattern showed apparent authority, estoppel, and ratification, and showed that notice of the real limits ends reasonable reliance.
The court found apparent authority and estoppel as well.
Lack of actual authority was not the end of the analysis.
B is correct.
topic: 2 · Contract liability & authority — Three theories, one case

q: In Lamkin v. Brooks, a town police officer returned to punch a drunk man who had threatened him at a call. Why was the town vicariously liable?
o: It was closely tied to his police duties.
Because the town ratified the punch.
Because police officers are strictly liable for all their acts.
Because the officer was an independent contractor.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Employment-rooted violence falls within scope. (The town's insurer escaped under an intentional-acts exclusion.)
The town did not ratify it.
No such rule applies.
He was an employee; that was not the theory.
A is correct.
topic: 3 · Tort liability of the principal — Lamkin's officer

q: Why did the court in Young v. Jones reject partnership by estoppel against the U.S. Price Waterhouse firm?
o: Because the two firms were in different countries.
Because partnership by estoppel has been abolished.
No one relied on any representation of partnership.
Because the U.S. firm had filed a statement denying partnership.
None of the above.
oe: Geography was not the reason.
It survives in UPA § 16 and RUPA § 308.
Correct. Worldwide-firm advertising was not enough without reliance by these plaintiffs.
No such statement was the basis of the holding.
C is correct.
topic: 6 · Partnership basics & formation — No partnership by estoppel

q: Under RUPA § 401(i), may a partner use partnership property for personal purposes?
o: Yes, freely, because each partner co-owns it.
Only on behalf of the partnership.
Yes, so long as the partner pays fair rent afterward.
Only with the consent of a majority of partners.
None of the above.
oe: Under RUPA a partner is not a co-owner of partnership property (§ 501).
Correct (§§ 401(i), 409(b)(1)(B)). Disotell v. Stiltner required a partner to account for personal use of partnership property during winding up.
Paying afterward does not make the use authorized.
Personal use outside the ordinary course would need more than a majority.
B is correct.
topic: 8 · Management & authority — Using partnership property

q: What is the common structure for real estate limited partnerships mentioned in class, and why is it used?
o: A corporate sole general partner, so no individual has unlimited liability.
The investors serve as general partners and a corporation as the limited partner.
All partners are individuals, so that the IRS will treat the LP as a corporation.
The LP has no general partner at all.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. The corporate general partner's shareholders are shielded by the corporation, and the investors by limited-partner status (Frigidaire).
This reverses the roles.
Tax classification is not the purpose.
An LP must have at least one general partner.
A is correct.
topic: 13 · LPs, LLPs & limited liability — Corporate general partner

q: During winding up, may a partner demand that a specific partnership asset be distributed to them in kind?
o: No; distributions are paid in money.
Yes, any partner may demand their share of each asset in kind.
Yes, if the asset was contributed by that partner.
Only if a majority consents.
None of the above.
oe: Correct (RUPA §§ 405(c), 806(f)). The partnership sells assets and distributes cash.
That would treat partners as co-owners of specific property, which RUPA rejects.
Contributed property belongs to the partnership; the partner has a claim to the value of the contribution.
There is no such default right.
A is correct.
topic: 7 · Partners’ economic rights & property — Distributions in money

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Comparing entities. Each question asks how the same event plays out across business forms under the default rules of the UPA (1914), the RUPA, and the ULLCA.

An owner dies. In which form does the death, by itself, dissolve the business by default?
o: A general partnership governed by the UPA.
A general partnership at will governed by the RUPA.
An LLC under the ULLCA.
A corporation.
None of the above.
oe: Correct. Under the UPA's aggregate theory, any partner's death dissolves the partnership (§ 31(4)), though the business may be continued by a new firm.
Death dissociates the partner. Under § 801(1), only express will to withdraw dissolves an at-will partnership; otherwise the firm buys out the estate.
A member's death dissociates the member but does not dissolve the LLC.
Shareholders' deaths do not affect a corporation's existence.
A is correct.
topic: 10 · Dissociation & dissolution — An owner dies

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Comparing entities. Each question asks how the same event plays out across business forms under the default rules of the UPA (1914), the RUPA, and the ULLCA.

An owner wants to leave and be paid for their stake. Under the default rules, which owner has a statutory right to be bought out?
o: A member of an LLC under the ULLCA.
A RUPA partner whose exit does not dissolve the firm.
A shareholder in a corporation, who may demand redemption at any time.
A partner in a UPA partnership, who may demand going-concern value.
None of the above.
oe: No buyout right: the departing member becomes a transferee (§ 603(a)(3)).
Correct. Article 7 requires the partnership to buy the interest (§ 701). This exit right is a selection factor favoring the partnership form.
Shareholders have no default right to be bought out.
The UPA remedy was liquidation, not a going-concern buyout.
B is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Cashing out

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Comparing entities. Each question asks how the same event plays out across business forms under the default rules of the UPA (1914), the RUPA, and the ULLCA.

In which forms is each owner, by default, an agent of the entity for acts apparently in the ordinary course of its business?
o: In every form, including the LLC and the limited partnership.
In the general partnership and the LLC.
The general partnership and the LLP.
In the LLC only.
None of the above.
oe: LLC members and limited partners are not agents by status.
An LLC member is not an agent solely by being a member (ULLCA § 301).
Correct. RUPA § 301 makes every partner an agent, and an LLP is still a general partnership. The shield limits liability, not authority.
The ULLCA removed status-based agency for members.
C is correct.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Owners as agents

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Comparing entities. Each question asks how the same event plays out across business forms under the default rules of the UPA (1914), the RUPA, and the ULLCA.

An owner's personal creditor wants to reach the owner's stake in the business. Which of the following statements are true?
o: In a RUPA partnership and in an LLC, the creditor's remedy is a charging order on the owner's distributions.
The creditor cannot seize specific assets of the entity, because of entity shielding.
In a single-member LLC, a court may order foreclosure, passing the entire interest to the buyer.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: True (RUPA § 504; ULLCA § 503).
True. Affirmative asset partitioning protects the firm's assets from owners' creditors.
True (ULLCA § 503).
Incomplete. C is also true.
Correct. Charging orders, entity shielding, and the single-member foreclosure exception work together.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — An owner's creditor

q:
Q7–11 FOCUS: Comparing entities. Each question asks how the same event plays out across business forms under the default rules of the UPA (1914), the RUPA, and the ULLCA.

By default, which of the following owners are personally liable for the entity's contract debts?
o: General partners of a general partnership.
General partners of an ordinary limited partnership.
Members of an LLC.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: Liable (RUPA § 306(a)).
Liable. Only limited partners are shielded, unless the LP is an LLLP.
Not liable (ULLCA § 304).
Correct. General partners carry unlimited liability in both forms; LLC members do not.
LLC members are shielded.
topic: 5 · Choosing an entity — Liability for contract debts

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duties of care, obedience, and disclosure, remedies for breach, and the principal's duties to the agent, under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.07–8.15) and the Restatement (Second).

An agent's principal instructs the agent to do something unlawful. What does the duty of obedience require?
o: The agent must obey every instruction the principal gives.
Obey lawful, reasonable instructions only.
The agent may ignore any instruction the agent disagrees with.
The agent must resign rather than refuse.
None of the above.
oe: The duty reaches only reasonable, lawful instructions.
Correct (R3d § 8.09; R2d § 385). An agent who disobeys a lawful instruction is liable for the resulting loss.
Disagreement does not excuse disobedience of a lawful instruction.
Refusing an unlawful instruction does not require resigning.
B is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Obedience

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duties of care, obedience, and disclosure, remedies for breach, and the principal's duties to the agent, under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.07–8.15) and the Restatement (Second).

What limits an agent's duty under R3d § 8.11 to give the principal information?
o: Nothing; the agent must disclose every fact it learns.
The agent may withhold any fact it considers unimportant.
The agent need disclose only facts learned in writing.
A superior duty owed to someone else.
None of the above.
oe: The duty covers facts the principal would want or that are material, and it has limits.
The test is what the principal would want to know, not the agent's preference.
How the agent learned a fact does not matter.
Correct. Section 8.11 requires reasonable efforts to provide material facts unless doing so would violate a superior duty owed to another person.
D is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Limits on disclosure

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duties of care, obedience, and disclosure, remedies for breach, and the principal's duties to the agent, under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.07–8.15) and the Restatement (Second).

Which of the following are remedies for an agent's breach of the duty of loyalty?
o: Disgorgement of the agent's profits.
A constructive trust over property the agent acquired.
Withholding compensation for an intentional breach.
A and B.
A, B and C.
oe: A remedy (Reading v. Regem; General Automotive v. Singer).
A remedy.
A remedy.
Incomplete. Forfeiting compensation is also available.
Correct. Principals may also seek an accounting, damages, and injunctions (R2d §§ 399–404).
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Remedies for disloyalty

q:
Q12–15 FOCUS: The agent's duties of care, obedience, and disclosure, remedies for breach, and the principal's duties to the agent, under the Restatement (Third) (§§ 8.07–8.15) and the Restatement (Second).

Why might a principal prefer to sue an agent for breach of fiduciary duty rather than breach of contract?
o: Fiduciary claims are always easier to settle.
Contract claims require a writing, while fiduciary claims do not.
Broader duties and remedies, without proof of loss.
Fiduciary claims have no statute of limitations.
None of the above.
oe: Settlement value is not the doctrinal reason.
Oral contracts can be enforced too.
Correct. Contract clauses (best efforts, conflict disclosure, non-competes) can handle the same risks in advance, but fiduciary remedies are broader after the fact.
Fiduciary claims are subject to limitation periods.
C is correct.
topic: 4 · Agents’ fiduciary duties — Fiduciary vs. contract claims
